Article Title: New York’s $95 million flood plan will turn parks, schoolyards and streets into hidden stormwater storage, an underground defence against extreme rainfall
Article Text:
New York’s Homecrest plan aims to capture stormwater before flooding

The quiet infrastructure designed to hold back heavy rain

The hidden effort to slow down stormwater during heavy rain

How New York is redesigning its response to extreme rainfall

The growing pressure on New York’s ageing drainage network

Protecting Coney Island Creek

Beneath parks, schoolyards, parking areas and other public spaces, New York is planning to create underground storage capable of holding stormwater before it overwhelms the sewer network. According to NYC Gov, the $95 million Homecrest project is part of a wider shift in how the city prepares for increasingly intense rainfall, using everyday public spaces as part of the drainage system rather than relying entirely on pipes and sewers.The project will cover roughly 350 acres around some of the neighbourhood’s most flood-prone streets and is designed for storms that can drop more than two inches of rain in an hour. Above ground, much may look unchanged. But during a sudden downpour, those familiar spaces could quietly become part of a hidden system designed to hold millions of gallons of water back from flooded streets and Coney Island Creek.The plan centres on a simple change in how rainwater is handled. Instead of sending every drop towards the existing sewer network as quickly as possible, some of it will be caught locally and held underground.That matters during short, intense storms, when the volume arriving on streets can rise very quickly. The Homecrest scheme is being designed around downpours capable of delivering more than two inches of rain in an hour. Those events can put considerable strain on drainage infrastructure, particularly in low-lying parts of southern Brooklyn.According to NYC Gov, the city says the project will cover about 350 acres, with work focused on known flooding trouble spots around Kings Highway, Coney Island Avenue and several of the surrounding avenues, including P, R, S, T, U and V.The city is working with its parks, transport and schools departments to identify public sites that can accommodate underground tanks. Traffic triangles, athletic courts, schoolyards and parking areas are among the places being assessed.The idea is to make use of land that already serves the neighbourhood without turning it into a conventional drainage facility. Water can be collected during a storm, stored below ground and dealt with later, after the immediate pressure on the drainage system has eased.Porous pavement forms another part of the scheme. Rather than allowing rain to sheet across an entirely sealed surface, permeable sections can let water move through the pavement and into systems beneath it.For residents, that could mean infrastructure that is easy to overlook on a dry day but performs a very different job when the rain arrives.Reportedly, DEP estimates that the completed Homecrest project will manage about 30 million gallons of stormwater annually.That figure is not the amount of water that will simply disappear. The purpose is to capture and temporarily store runoff so that less reaches the sewer network at the most difficult point of a storm.There is a second concern beyond flooded roads and overloaded drains. Rainwater flowing over streets can pick up oil, rubbish and other pollutants before reaching local waterways. In Homecrest, the project is also intended to reduce the amount of polluted runoff entering Coney Island Creek.New York began its Cloudburst Management Program in 2023, with the same broad principle being tested in several flood-prone neighbourhoods.Projects are under way or being advanced in places including Parkchester in the Bronx, Brownsville and East New York in Brooklyn, East Harlem in Manhattan, and Corona, Jamaica, Kissena and St. Albans in Queens.The approach reflects a shift away from relying solely on traditional underground sewer capacity. New infrastructure can still involve pipes and drains, but the city is also looking at streets, parks and other public land as part of the stormwater system.Homecrest is one of the larger commitments under that programme, with $95 million in DEP funding allocated to the project.The timing of the investment is tied to a practical problem facing the city's drainage network. Short bursts of very heavy rain can overwhelm systems that may cope perfectly well with more moderate rainfall spread over a longer period.The Homecrest project is being designed specifically for those cloudburst conditions. Rather than trying to move all the water away immediately, the system is intended to slow it down and create somewhere for it to go.That approach is particularly relevant in southern Brooklyn, where residents and local officials have repeatedly raised concerns about flooding during major storms. The memory of Hurricane Sandy also remains part of the area's experience with extreme weather.The city has described the investment as part of a broader effort to strengthen neighbourhoods against increasingly intense rainfall while protecting waterways from untreated runoff.Flood management is not the only environmental objective behind the project. During intense rainfall, runoff can move quickly from roads and other hard surfaces into the sewer network or nearby waterways.Capturing some of that water before it reaches those routes can reduce the amount of contaminated runoff entering Coney Island Creek. The city says this will help improve water quality and support its obligations under the federal Clean Water Act.That makes the project less about simply keeping particular streets dry. It is also about controlling what happens to rainwater after it hits the ground.
Article Summary: $95 million Homecrest project is part of a wider shift in how the city prepares for increasingly intense rainfall. Project will cover roughly 350 acres around some of the neighbourhood’s most flood-prone streets. Water can be collected during a storm, stored below ground and dealt with later, after the immediate pressure on the drainage system has eased.

Article Title: Israel accuses Gaza of launching drones, balloons and kites; responds with two airstrikes killing four-year old
Article Text:
Four-year-old boy among 2 killed in Gaza airstrikes

At least two people, including a four-year-old boy, were killed and seven others wounded in two Israeli airstrikes in the Gaza Strip on Sunday.This comes as Israel threatened to intensify attacks following what it said were launches of balloons, drones and kites from Gaza towards Israel.One of the strikes hit a building in the central town of Zawayda after the Israeli army warned the property’s owners to evacuate, residents said.Medics said flying debris and shrapnel scattered over an area spanning dozens of metres, injuring at least six people, including four-year-old Mohammad Abdel-Salam Taha, who was later pronounced dead at a hospital.“There is no ceasefire, there is nothing,” said Abu Ahmed, a displaced Palestinian sheltering near the building, which the airstrike reduced to a pile of mangled steel and concrete."We want solutions, we want to live ​in peace," he added, as cited by Reuters.The second airstrike struck the nearby Nuseirat refugee camp, Palestinian health officials said.The strikes came as Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Israel would intensify targeted attacks against those responsible for launching drones, balloons and kites from the Gaza Strip if the launches did not stop immediately.Hamas, meanwhile, accused Israel of using children's kites as a pretext to escalate "attacks" on Gaza.In a post on X, the prime minister of Israel's official account said Netanyahu and defence minister Israel Katz held "a situational assessment this evening regarding the threat of drones, balloons and kites launched from the Gaza Strip toward Israel."The meeting was attended by Chief of the General Staff Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, the Head of the National Security Council and senior IDF officials.Israel issued a warning against Hamas that "if the launches toward Israel do not cease immediately, the IDF will act to increase targeted strikes against those responsible for the launches and will evacuate the population from areas used as launch sites for kites, drones, and balloons."The developments came as US special envoy Jared Kushner said Washington had made significant progress during a nearly four-hour meeting with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu on August 17.The discussions focused on Gaza’s reconstruction, demilitarisation and Israel’s security concerns.
Article Summary: At least two people, including a four-year-old boy, were killed and seven others wounded in two Israeli airstrikes in the Gaza Strip on Sunday. This comes as Israel threatened to intensify attacks following what it said were launches of balloons, drones and kites from Gaza towards Israel.

Article Title: UK PM Burnham to visit Kyiv as Ukraine turns 35, Britain to boost long-range strike capability
Article Text:
“After all, Ukraine’s security is our security”, said British Prime Minister Andy Burnham (Photo: AP).

UK to share missile technology

UK backs Ukraine amid war

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will visit Kyiv on Monday as Ukraine marks its 35th Independence Day, making it his first international trip since taking office last month.Burnham is expected to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and chair his first meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing”, an alliance of 34 countries formed by the UK and France in 2025 to support Ukraine with long-term military assistance, defence cooperation and post-ceasefire security guarantees."On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes”, Burnham said ahead of his visit.“After all, Ukraine’s security is our security”, he added.During his visit, Burnham is expected to announce government approval allowing defence company MBDA to release classified information and British components linked to SCALP long-range missiles to Ukraine, according to a statement from the UK prime minister's office.The development comes as Ukraine and France reportedly explore plans to establish local assembly lines for the missile in Ukraine.SCALP is the French version of the Storm Shadow long-range cruise missile and is jointly produced by Britain and France. The UK was the first country to provide Ukraine with long-range strike weapons in 2023, according to the prime minister's office.The announcement comes amid growing Ukrainian use of British-supplied drones against Russian infrastructure.Moscow has warned of "consequences" over the increasing use of the drones.Britain has remained one of Ukraine's strongest supporters since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.London has committed around £25 billion ($34 billion) in support for Ukraine, including £16 billion in military assistance, AFP reported.During Zelenskyy's earlier visit to the UK, London also announced plans to share information on its battle-tested electronic jammers known as "Stone Cloak".The tablet-sized systems can be attached to drones and are designed to disrupt Russian air defence systems, making it harder for them to track and target the weapons in flight, according to the UK prime minister's office.
Article Summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will visit Kyiv on Monday as Ukraine marks its 35th Independence Day. Burnham is expected to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and chair his first meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing’

Article Title: 'Did not meet launch conditions': China's unmanned moon mission delayed last minute
Article Text:
China has postponed the planned launch of its Chang'e-7 Moon mission, days after saying the launch site and equipment were in good condition.

China has postponed the planned launch of its Chang'e-7 Moon mission, days after saying the launch site and equipment were in good condition.The probe and the Long March 5 rocket assigned to carry it had already been transferred to the takeoff area at the Wenchang Space Launch Center in southern Hainan province last week. As of Wednesday, inspections were still due to be carried out and the agency said the launch was "scheduled for the coming period".On Sunday, China's manned space agency said a "comprehensive assessment" had found that the mission "does not meet launch conditions and cannot take place during the planned window this year". It did not identify which conditions had not been met or say when the mission could be rescheduled. Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported the announcement.Chang'e-7 is designed to search for water at the Moon's south pole. Media reports had indicated that it could lift off either over the weekend or on Monday.The agency said the postponement was "based on the principle of prudence, reliability and absolute mission success". It provided no further details behind the decision.The delay also comes just under two weeks after a rare launch failure from Wenchang.Media reports showed a rocket launched from the Hainan site exploding as crowds watched a fiery ball in the sky.State news agency Xinhua said the failed mission used a Long March 7A carrier rocket that had taken off from the Wenchang Space Launch Site. The rocket was carrying the Zhongxing-4B communications satellite when an "anomaly" occurred during flight.Xinhua said the cause of the failure remained under investigation.The two developments come as Beijing continues to expand its space programme, into which it has invested billions of dollars in recent years. President Xi Jinping has described the country's ambitions in space as its "space dream".China also successfully landed a reusable rocket for the first time in July, according to its space agency. The milestone represented an advance in China's space programme, including its efforts to reduce launch costs.Chang'e-7 forms part of China's wider push to put astronauts on the Moon before 2030. The United States is competing in the same race through its Artemis programme.
Article Summary: Chang'e-7 is designed to search for water at the Moon's south pole. Delay also comes just under two weeks after a rare launch failure from Wenchang. President Xi Jinping has described the country's ambitions in space as its "space dream"

Article Title: TikToker Ayesha Gilamana murder case takes shocking turn as police uncover family link
Article Text:

Police find possible family link in Ayesha Gilamana’s killing

Ayesha Gilamana case takes another shocking turn

“honour killing.”

TikTok star Ayesha Gilamana’s murder case has taken a shocking turn after police said they found a possible link to her own family. Gilamana, whose real name was Shamsoo Bibi, was shot dead in Taxila, Pakistan, on August 14. She was traveling in a car with her siblings when two men on a motorcycle opened fire. The 28-year-old had about 1.3 million TikTok followers and 176,000 YouTube subscribers. Police are now investigating claims that people close to her may have been involved in her death.Police in Rawalpindi said on August 22 that five people had been arrested in connection with Gilamana’s death. The group reportedly includes her father, Fazal Sahibzada, and her biological brother, Bashir.Police said they found the possible family link after checking technical evidence, CCTV footage and other information. Investigators reportedly looked at footage from more than 100 cameras while trying to understand what happened before and after the shooting.According to police, Gilamana’s father and brother allegedly told investigators that they helped arrange the killing with other suspects. However, these are police allegations, and the investigation is still going on.Gilamana’s father had first reported her death to police. At the time, he reportedly said she had been threatened because of a money dispute. He also named other people he believed could be behind the shooting.Police now claim that this story may have been created to make investigators look at people outside the family.Investigators have also claimed that Gilamana’s social media career had become a source of conflict inside her family. Police have described the suspected motive as an allegedPolice also said they found evidence of an earlier alleged attempt to attack Gilamana. According to investigators, a plan was made to target her while she was attending a wedding in Haripur. However, she reportedly changed her route and avoided the attack.On the day she was killed, Gilamana was traveling with her 15-year-old sister and another brother named Nematullah. Police have made it clear that Nematullah is not the same brother, Bashir, who has been arrested.The investigation is still underway. Police said they are continuing to work out the exact role of each person before sending the case to court.Gilamana’s death has shocked her large online audience. What first appeared to be a shooting linked to an outside dispute has now become a much bigger investigation, with police looking into possible involvement from people within her own family.
Article Summary: Ayesha Gilamana was shot dead in Taxila, Pakistan, on August 14. The 28-year-old had about 1.3 million TikTok followers and 176,000 YouTube subscribers. Police are now investigating claims that people close to her may have been involved in her death.

Article Title: TikTok food influencer Doctor Food arrested in Lebanon over alleged drug-linked food products
Article Text:
Image/X

TikTok food influencer Doctor Food arrested in Lebanon after police search

Doctor Food faces alleged drug-linked food products case

TikTok food influencer Georges Dib, known online as Doctor Food, has been arrested in Lebanon over alleged drug-related crimes involving food products made by businesses linked to him. Dib has more than eight million TikTok followers and is known for sharing food, cooking and lifestyle videos. Lebanese authorities said he was arrested on August 23 after a month-long search. Police had reportedly been looking for him for years. He had also previously been sentenced to life in prison in absentia over alleged drug trafficking Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces said Dib was arrested after officers spent about a month investigating and watching his movements.Police eventually raided his home in the Rahbeh area of Akkar, northern Lebanon, and arrested him. Authorities said Dib was wanted under two court warrants connected to a drug-related case.Police also claimed that Dib had been trying to avoid being found while continuing to make videos for his large social media audience.According to investigators, he would record his content and then leave his home. Police said he also changed vehicles and phone numbers often, which they believe was done to make it harder for them to track him.Dib was later handed over to the relevant authorities for further legal action.The case goes back to an earlier investigation at Beirut’s international airport. Lebanese authorities reportedly seized confectionery and other food products that allegedly contained narcotics.The products were said to have been made at factories owned by Dib’s businesses. Investigators reportedly believed the products were being prepared for shipment to a Gulf country.Dib was accused of making, trafficking and smuggling drugs outside Lebanon. He had previously been sentenced to life in prison in absentia over drug trafficking allegations.A judicial source told AFP that Dib is expected to be moved to a detention center in Mount Lebanon. He is also expected to face another trial over additional alleged drug trafficking charges.Despite the earlier case, Dib continued posting videos on TikTok and remained active online. After reports about his previous conviction appeared in July, he denied the accusations in a video and asked his followers not to believe the claims being made about him.Doctor Food has built a large online audience through videos about food, restaurants and his daily life. His arrest now puts his social media career and business activities under a major legal spotlight.The investigation and court proceedings are still continuing. The allegations against Dib have not been proven in court, and he will have the opportunity to respond to the charges through the legal process.
Article Summary: Georges Dib, known online as Doctor Food, has been arrested in Lebanon over alleged drug-related crimes. Dib has more than eight million TikTok followers and is known for sharing food, cooking and lifestyle videos. Lebanese authorities said he was arrested on August 23 after a month-long search. He is also expected to face another trial over additional alleged drug trafficking charges.

Article Title: Ex-Pakistan PM Imran Khan returns to Adiala Jail after medical examination at Islamabad hospital
Article Text:
73-year-old cricket legend facing health issues after 3 years of imprisonment

Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan on Friday returned to Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail shortly after undergoing a medical examination at Shifa Hospital in Islamabad.The development was confirmed to Reuters by a member of his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.The 73-year-old cricket legend has been facing health issues after spending more than three years in prison following his tenure as prime minister.Khan was taken to Shifa Hospital days after the Supreme Court ordered a medical examination. An official from the Shehbaz Sharif-led government said Islamabad was complying with the Supreme Court's order to facilitate his medical examination.Khan's party and family had sought permission for him to remain in hospital.A three-judge Supreme Court panel had ordered authorities two days earlier to take Khan to Shifa International Hospital for a medical examination amid prolonged concerns raised by his family and personal doctors over his health and access to treatment.The court directed that a medical board, including specialists and his personal physician, Faisal Sultan, examine him.The Supreme Court's order came after former Pakistan president Arif Alvi shared Khan's vitals and raised concerns over what he described as "alarming" medical reports.In a post on X, Alvi said, "Imran Khan's medical reports are alarming. I have gone through them with several specialists, and I am writing this in plain language so every Pakistani can understand exactly what is happening."Alvi also highlighted Khan's health concerns, citing his "anxiety and stress levels", "palpitations," and "high blood pressure." He added that while sleeplessness was not mentioned in the report, Khan's medication appeared to suggest the problem.
Article Summary: Imran Khan returned to Adiala Jail after medical examination at Shifa Hospital in Islamabad. Khan, 73, has been facing health issues after spending more than three years in prison following his tenure as prime minister. A three-judge Supreme Court panel had ordered authorities two days earlier to take Khan to Shifa International Hospital for a medical examination.

Article Title: US debt crosses $40 trillion but everyone still trusts Uncle Sam. But for how long?
Article Text:
US national debt crossed $40 trillion, exceeding annual GDP, as interest payments approach $1 trillion, with economists warning of painful adjustments ahead.

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Amid The Urge To Splurge, Trump Has Proposed Hike Of 50% In Def Budget

Surprisingly, America is not mainly borrowing from China. The biggest lenders are actually Americans and American institutions – pension funds, mutual funds, banks, insurance companies, households and investment funds. Foreign governments and investors also buy what is euphemistically called “US Treasury securities”: Japan held about $1.12 trillion in June, Britain about $940 billion, China about $633 billion and India roughly $200 billion.

Yes, Uncle Sam, we’ll take your IOU.

The United States’ national debt crossed $40 trillion on Tuesday, a number so large that even breaking it up with commas can scarcely make it comprehensible. As in a 4 followed by 13 zeroes: $40,000,000,000,000!Number-crunching economists reached for various metrics to convey the scale of the crisis. The US economy produces roughly $33 trillion worth of goods and services a year. So the debt is now bigger than the entire annual economic output (GDP) of the country. Per American, that works out to roughly $118,000; for a family of four, about $472,000. Divvying it another way, the US is adding debt at a rate of roughly $90,000 every second.To put that in perspective for readers in India, the $40 trillion debt America has racked up is roughly 10 times the size of India’s entire annual economy. In other words — although debt versus GDP is not an apples-to-apples comparison — the US owes roughly ten times the value of everything India produces in a year. America’s debt mountain is therefore not merely bigger than India’s economy; it is about ten Indian economies stacked on top of one another.Economists also put the best possible spin by pointing out that the raw number itself is less important than debt relative to the size of the economy and the government’s ability to service it.Just the US debt held by its public is roughly equal to annual GDP, and the Congressional Budget Office says that, under current law, the ratio could rise to 120% of GDP by 2036 and 175% by 2056.So how did the world’s richest country get here? In the simplest terms, Washington has been spending more than it collects in taxes — year after year, administration after administration. Wars, tax cuts, the 2008 financial crisis, Covid stimulus, an ageing population and rising Social Security and Medicare costs have all added to the bill. The pandemic was particularly spectacular: debt exploded as the government tried to prevent an economic catastrophe.But the extraordinary thing is that America has continued borrowing heavily even after the emergencies have passed. Federal budget deficits are still running at levels normally associated with wars or recessions. The awkward question for Washington now is whether the borrowing eventually stops gently — or with a crash.So who is lending America $40 trillion?But why lend to a country this deeply in debt? Because US “Treasury securities” remain the world’s favourite financial equivalent of a steel safe with a very large lock. They are highly liquid, easily traded and backed by the world’s largest economy — as well as by Washington’s long-established record of paying its debts. In other words, America has been able to borrow on an extraordinary scale because the world keeps saying:For now.President Trump has repeatedly promised to reduce the national debt, including by using tariff revenue. But the arithmetic has not exactly been taking orders from the White House. Amid the irresistible American urge to splurge, Trump is proposing a $1.5 trillion military budget, roughly a 50% increase from recent levels and an unprecedented level of Pentagon spending, arguing that a stronger military is essential to national security.So America is essentially trying to lose weight while ordering a second dessert; spending like a drunken sailor on shore leave — and then promising the bartender that tariffs will somehow pay the tab.And debt is not merely about the amount borrowed. It is also about the interest bill. Interest payments are now approaching $1 trillion a year. That means an increasing share of the federal budget is going simply toward servicing yesterday’s borrowing rather than paying for today’s schools, roads, defence, healthcare or anything else Washington wants to spend money on.As the debt grows, investors could eventually demand higher interest rates to keep buying Treasury securities. That would feed through into mortgage rates, business borrowing costs and the government’s own financing costs, potentially slowing investment and economic growth. The US would then face the unpleasant menu economists have been warning about for years: higher taxes, slower spending, cuts to benefits, faster economic growth, inflation — or some combination of all of them.Washington would have to bring spending and revenues into better balance: restrain the growth of entitlement programmes, control discretionary spending, reconsider tax cuts, raise more revenue and — hardest of all — persuade voters that there is no painless option. There is no magic button marked “Pay Off $40 Trillion.”The CBO’s is essentially warning that the longer Washington waits, the more painful the eventual adjustment becomes. That is America’s peculiar fiscal paradox: the world’s richest country can afford an enormous debt — until one day the debt becomes so enormous that it starts deciding what the world’s richest country can afford. Or as one economist might put it, there is no such thing as a free lunch -- just a lunch somebody has put on the national credit card.
Article Summary: US national debt crossed $40 trillion, exceeding annual GDP, as interest payments approach $1 trillion, with economists warning of painful adjustments ahead. To put that in perspective for readers in India, the $40 trillions debt America has racked up is roughly 10 times the size of India’s entire annual economy.

Article Title: Japan installed a 1.1 MW turbine beneath the Naru Strait, using predictable tidal currents to generate clean electricity for the Goto Islands
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How Japan’s 1.1 MW AR1100 tidal turbine generates electricity underwater

Image AI generated

Japan’s tidal energy project grows from a 500 kW pilot to a 1.1 MW turbine

Why predictable tidal energy could complement solar and wind in Japan

The engineering challenges of operating a tidal turbine underwater

Between Japan’s Goto Islands, the sea is doing something that is usually associated with wind farms and solar fields. Beneath the surface of the Naru Strait, a 1.1 MW turbine is drawing energy from water moving with the tides and sending electricity back towards land through a subsea cable. No blades are turning in the sky and no panels spread across the shoreline. The machine works largely out of sight, following currents whose timing can be forecast well in advance. Installed by Proteus Marine Renewables, the AR1100 grew from an earlier 500 kW trial in the same waters. Its deployment has given Japan a megawatt-scale tidal system designed to work with the regular rise and fall of the sea rather than depending on sunshine or changing winds.The project also demonstrates the potential of tidal power in narrow channels, where fast-moving water can provide a concentrated source of renewable energy. By placing the turbine underwater, the system avoids taking up large areas of land while tapping into a resource that follows a predictable natural cycle.Unlike solar and wind power, tidal energy has one major advantage: its timing can be predicted years ahead because tides follow the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun.That predictability could make tidal turbines useful alongside renewable sources whose output changes with weather conditions.The AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water and no set of panels covering land. The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection. According to Proteus Marine Renewables, the turbine was deployed in February 2025, while later company information recorded that it received Japanese certification and began exporting electricity to the grid in June 2025.The arrangement is fairly straightforward in principle, although operating it beneath the sea is not. The rotor extracts energy from moving water, the drivetrain passes that mechanical power to a permanent-magnet generator, and the resulting electricity is carried to an onshore station. A yaw system turns the nacelle as the tidal flow reverses, while independently controlled blades can alter their pitch to regulate how the turbine responds to changing conditions. AR1100 is a horizontal-axis turbine mounted on a gravity-based support structure. The earlier project in the same strait provided the starting point for the larger machine.Offshore Energy reported that the earlier 500 kW AR500 pilot operated in the Naru Strait with 97% availability in 2021. That earlier machine had a rated capacity of 500 kW and recorded 97% availability during its operation, according to the material released about the project. The experience allowed engineers to see how the technology behaved in the actual marine environment rather than only in controlled testing.The next version increased the rated capacity to 1.1 MW and introduced changes to the turbine's control systems. An equipment supply and works contract with Kyuden Mirai Energy was signed in November 2022, with the Japanese project subsequently moving towards the upgraded machine. Advanced pitch and yaw systems were incorporated as part of the work. The company says those changes were intended to improve the turbine's performance and efficiency while allowing it to deal more effectively with the changing direction of the tidal flow.The most distinctive feature of tidal power is not simply that the turbines sit underwater. It is the predictability of the resource. Solar output changes with daylight and weather conditions. Wind can strengthen, weaken or stop altogether. ClickPetroleogas noted that tidal production can be estimated in advance because the cycles follow predictable natural patterns, unlike renewable generation that is more affected by weather conditions. The electricity produced at any particular moment still depends on the conditions at the site and the performance of the equipment; the underlying movement of the water is far less of a surprise.That distinction matters when renewable sources are being combined. A grid operator cannot make the sun shine or order the wind to blow, whereas the timing of tidal cycles can be incorporated into generation planning. It does not make tidal energy constant; the flow rises and falls as the tide changes, but it makes the pattern easier to anticipate. For islands such as those around the Goto group, where space and fuel logistics can present particular constraints, a submerged source can sit alongside solar, wind and other forms of generation. The Naru Strait project is intended to contribute to reducing emissions from the islands' electricity supply.Underwater generation creates its own engineering problems. Components have to survive saltwater, strong currents and long periods of exposure while remaining accessible enough for inspection and maintenance. Getting people and equipment to a submerged turbine can also require vessels, specialist crews and careful planning. The location itself has to provide sufficient water movement, suitable depth and a practical route for sending the electricity into the grid.The Naru Strait project therefore depends on more than the turbine turning. Its subsea cable links the machine to an onshore electrical station, where the generated power can be processed for distribution. Local vessels and resources were used during deployment, with Proteus' offshore team overseeing the work, while Kyuden Mirai Energy and Japan's Ministry of Environment have been involved in advancing the project.There is also a useful way to think about the long-term promise of the machine, without treating its output as something that can be guaranteed hour by hour. The tidal timetable itself is highly predictable. Engineers can calculate when stronger and weaker currents are expected well into the future, creating a generation pattern that can be plotted ahead of time. What cannot simply be printed on that chart is the turbine's actual electricity production for every future hour: maintenance, operating conditions and other technical factors still matter.That distinction is important. The Naru Strait turbine is not a giant power station, nor does the available source material establish that it will produce a fixed amount of electricity every hour for a decade. What the project demonstrates is something more specific: a megawatt-scale machine can be installed beneath a Japanese strait, connected to shore and operated using an energy source whose basic timing is known far in advance. The water will keep changing direction. The turbine is built to follow it.
Article Summary: The AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water. The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Dwayne Johnson: "Be humble. Be hungry. And always be..." - a lesson on staying successful
Article Text:
Dwayne Johnson

Quote of the day by Dwayne Johnson

"Be humble. Be hungry. And always be the hardest worker in the room."

Dwayne Johnson’s success story is really about starting again

A simple way to actually use this idea

Other famous quotes by Dwayne Johnson

"Success isn't always about greatness. It's about consistency . Consistent hard work leads to success. Greatness will come."

. Consistent leads to success. Greatness will come." "If you have a dream, chase it. Because a dream doesn't work unless you do."

"The struggles along the way are only meant to shape you for your purpose."

Two people can reach a comparable level of success and carry themselves in completely different ways once they get there. One starts believing their own reputation, coasting on past results and expecting continued recognition without continued effort. The other keeps behaving, day to day, as though the position they've reached is still something to be earned rather than something already secured. Johnson, an actor and former professional wrestler who built one of the most consistently bankable careers in modern entertainment, has repeated some version of this line across interviews and public talks for years, treating it less as a motivational slogan and more as an operating discipline he applies to himself regardless of how much he's already accomplished. The three instructions build on each other deliberately: humility to keep success from distorting self-perception, hunger to keep ambition from going stale once a goal is reached, and outworking everyone else in the room as the concrete, checkable behaviour that proves the first two aren't just talk. His remarkable career trajectory proves that sustained success requires continuously earning respect through consistent effort, rather than simply resting on past achievements and accumulated reputation.What gives this line extra weight is how directly it maps onto Johnson's own well-documented history. Before wrestling or acting, he was cut from the Canadian Football League after a brief and unsuccessful professional football career, a setback that reportedly left him with only a few dollars to his name and forced him to move back in with his parents to rebuild from there. He then built a wrestling career from the ground up, working through years of small venues and modest paydays before becoming one of the most recognisable performers in WWE history.That same pattern repeated when he transitioned to acting, starting in supporting and low-budget roles before working his way, over roughly two decades, into becoming one of the highest-paid actors in the world. Johnson has spoken repeatedly about maintaining an intense personal work ethic, including famously early gym sessions and a demanding schedule, even at the peak of his commercial success, treating each new project as something that still has to be earned rather than something his existing fame should simply guarantee him.The useful move here is treating each of the three instructions as a separate check rather than a single vague attitude, since it's entirely possible to stay humble while quietly losing hunger, or to stay hungry while letting effort slide once recognition arrives. Humility alone can drift into complacency if nothing keeps pushing forward. Hunger alone can curdle into arrogance if nothing keeps it grounded. The third instruction, being the hardest worker in the room, is what actually forces the first two to remain honest rather than becoming things a person merely claims about themselves.A fair test, at any point success starts to feel comfortable, is to ask honestly whether the current level of effort would still hold up if nobody already knew your track record. That question won't manufacture motivation out of nothing. It usually reveals how much of the current effort is riding on reputation rather than on work still actually being done.
Article Summary: Dwayne Johnson is an actor and former professional wrestler. His quote of the day is about consistency and being the hardest worker in the room. Johnson has spoken repeatedly about maintaining an intense personal work ethic. He treats each new project as something that still has to be earned.

Article Title: A 175-year-old New Jersey family farm faced a 130-home housing plan; after six years of fighting, the owners kept the land
Article Text:
PC:Henry family

Cranbury’s 175-year-old New Jersey farm faced eminent domain for affordable housing

Henry family challenges Cranbury’s eminent domain plan in court

October 2025 settlement saves Cranbury’s 175-year-old Henry family farm

For 175 years, the Henry family farm in Cranbury, New Jersey, remained a working piece of farmland. But in 2025, the 175-year-old property found itself at the centre of a dispute over the state's push to provide more affordable housing. Cranbury Township planned to acquire part of the 21-acre farm for a 130-unit housing development, warning the owners that it could use eminent domain if they refused to sell. What followed was a prolonged legal and political fight that drew in residents, state leaders and federal officials. The Henry family challenged the proposed taking in court while the township faced growing pressure to find another location for its housing obligation. A change to a state rule governing the distance between affordable housing and warehouses eventually opened the door to an alternative site. By October 2025, a settlement had been reached, removing the farm from the housing plan and allowing the property to remain with the family. The owners are now working to place the land under farmland preservation protections.The proposed development was not simply a planning idea. LegalClarity reported that the township sent the Henry brothers a letter in April 2025 warning that it would use eminent domain if they did not agree to sell.The Township Committee then voted unanimously in May to authorise eminent domain proceedings. The proposed housing project was to include six multi-family buildings, a community building and open space, with homes designated for very-low-, low- and moderate-income households.The decision triggered a strong local backlash. Residents attended committee meetings to protest the proposed seizure, while former mayor Jay Taylor raised concerns about property rights and the farm's importance as an environmental buffer in an area increasingly surrounded by warehouses. Andy Henry said the “farm represents exactly what the town prides itself on”, pointing to its open space, history and farmhouse. The dispute soon moved beyond Cranbury, attracting attention from state politicians and federal officials.The Henry family took the fight into court. Their attorney, Timothy Duggan, challenged the proposed taking on several grounds, arguing that the property was intended to be transferred to a private developer rather than used for genuine public use. Other arguments questioned how the township had selected the site, whether the rights of other property owners had been treated equally and whether the developer had been given an improper role in choosing the land. Andy Henry also filed a separate lawsuit against the eminent domain ordinance, while Henry Realty Co. challenged the township's housing plan.At the same time, a seemingly technical housing regulation became central to the dispute. New Jersey's Housing and Mortgage Finance Agency had required affordable housing sites to be at least 250 feet from a warehouse facility's property line. Cranbury officials argued that this rule had eliminated many possible alternatives. In August 2025, however, township officials went before the agency and pushed for the way the buffer was measured to be changed. Negotiations involving the Henry family, Cranbury Township and the Fair Share Housing Centre followed, with federal and state officials also becoming involved.The breakthrough came in October 2025, when Governor Phil Murphy announced that a settlement had been reached. “For 175 years, the Henry Family Farm has stood on South River Road in Cranbury as a proud symbol of that agricultural tradition,” Murphy said. “New Jersey will always protect its farmers and farmland.” The settlement became possible after the housing agency revised its warehouse buffer rule, measuring the 250-foot distance from the actual “area of warehouse operations” rather than the entire warehouse property's boundary.The change allowed Cranbury to consider other land for its housing obligations. The Henry farm was ultimately removed from the housing plan, while a new 11.82-acre site at 1260 South River Road was selected for the proposed 130-unit affordable development. The amended plan was later approved, and the farm remained under Henry family ownership. Andy Henry said that after regaining control of the property, the family was working to place it in New Jersey's Farmland Preservation Program to prevent future development attempts. His attorney also helped facilitate the farm's entry into the programme.
Article Summary: Cranbury Township planned to acquire part of the 21-acre farm for a 130-unit housing development. The Henry family challenged the proposed taking in court while the township faced pressure to find another location for its housing obligation. A change to a state rule governing the distance between affordable housing and warehouses eventually opened the door to an alternative site.

Article Title: Nevada wildfire: 90,000 people face evacuation as state of emergency declared
Article Text:
The 'Hawk Fire' began on Saturday

Governor declares state of emergency

New fires pop up

(With AP inputs)

A fast-growing wildfire in northwest Reno, Nevada, remained uncontained and was determined to be human-caused, authorities said Sunday. Officials expanded the “GO NOW” evacuation zone and urged about 90,000 people to evacuate or prepare to leave.About 42,000 residents were under evacuation orders, while another 45,000 were in an adjacent evacuation warning zone. Authorities urged everyone in both areas to leave and be prepared to remain away for several days, warning that shifting, strengthening winds could make the fire increasingly unpredictable.The "Hawk Fire" began on Saturday and quickly grew to about 20 square miles (53 sq km) as it spread through the Peavine Peak area of the Humboldt–Toiyabe National Forest, where rugged foothills are surrounded by homes and businesses near the California state line.The blaze advanced exceptionally quickly, jumping over fire trucks and hampering firefighters’ efforts to reach hotspots as residents fled the area.Several structures were destroyed, and six people — three civilians and three first responders — were injured. Authorities did not provide further details about the fire’s cause, saying the investigation was ongoing.Nevada governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and mobilised the Nevada National Guard to support aerial firefighting operations with two helicopter crews.Another 60 troops were deployed to help law enforcement secure evacuated neighborhoods.Nearly 10,000 customers remained without power, down from about 60,000 on Saturday. Portions of US Route 395, a major north-south highway, were also closed because of the fire. Reno, with more than 280,000 residents, is Nevada’s largest city outside the Las Vegas metropolitan area.Washoe County emergency officials opened the Reno-Sparks Convention Center to evacuees but asked them not to bring pets. Separate shelters were designated for small and large animals. Reno casinos also offered discounted hotel rooms to people displaced by the fire.Nevada saw 15 new fires on Saturday alone. Earlier this month, wildfires in eastern Washington state forced about 60,000 people to evacuate the Spokane area, while three wildfires north of Reno displaced more than 13,000 residents.Meanwhile, communities just outside the evacuation zone remained on alert.The University of Nevada, Reno, where many of its 20,000 undergraduate students moved into campus housing over the weekend, was just outside the evacuation zone Sunday.Two hospitals evacuated patients, while the sheriff’s office closely monitored conditions to determine whether the county jail would also need to be evacuated.
Article Summary: The "Hawk Fire" began on Saturday and quickly grew to about 20 square miles (53 sq km) as it spread through the Peavine Peak area of the Humboldt–Toiyabe National Forest. Officials expanded the “GO NOW’ evacuation zone and urged about 90,000 people to evacuate or prepare to leave.

Article Title: In 1959, a California teenager began building a castle from bottles, car parts and scrap metal; decades later, it had towers and a giant clock
Article Text:
PC: wikipedia

How the Albourne Rancho and Glendora scrap yard shaped Michael Rubel’s castle project

How Michael Rubel built Rubel Castle from salvaged materials

What can you see inside Rubel Castle in California

How Glendora’s citrus-farming past became part of Rubel Castle

In the foothills of Southern California, an unusual castle grew out of materials that most people would have thrown away. Bottles, scrap metal, old machinery, car parts and fragments of Glendora’s past were collected and worked into a sprawling handmade complex that took decades to complete. Michael Clarke Rubel began the project when he was just 19, drawing on a childhood habit of building makeshift forts from discarded objects. Over the following 26 years, he mixed concrete almost every day, adding towers, walls and other structures to the site. The finished Rubel Castle is not a replica of a European fortress, but a distinctly Californian creation shaped by the town around it. Its towers rise from a former citrus-growing landscape, while a giant clock, bottle-filled buildings, tunnels and salvaged objects form part of the unusual site. Much of what Rubel used had once been destined for demolition, abandonment or the scrap yard.Michael Rubel had known the area around the old Albourne Rancho from childhood. According to the Glendora Historical Society, he worked odd jobs there when he was young and became familiar with its citrus-packing facilities and reservoir. He and other children also spent time collecting discarded materials from the municipal scrap yard, using whatever they could find to make improvised forts and castles.That early habit of turning unwanted objects into something else stayed with him. By the time the citrus groves and older agricultural buildings around Glendora were disappearing under suburban development, Rubel was looking at the remains differently. In 1959, aged 19, he bought the last remnant of the Albourne Rancho. What began as a childhood idea then became a project that would occupy much of his life. The historical society describes the finished site as a “one-of-a-kind monument” to Rubel’s imagination and to the people who helped him build it.Rubel did not build the castle by simply ordering conventional construction materials. Salvage became part of the process. Bottles, metal objects, machinery and other fragments gathered from around Glendora could be incorporated into the site, while friends, neighbours and relatives helped with the physical work. Rubel made a point of mixing at least a yard of concrete every day, gradually adding to the structures over a period of 26 years.The walls were constructed using river rock and Portland cement alongside pieces rescued from the town’s past. Some objects became part of the buildings themselves, while others were adapted for use elsewhere on the property. The construction therefore happened in a piecemeal way, with the site changing as Rubel found new materials and ideas. Towers eventually reached about 75 feet, while the wider property developed into much more than a single castle.Rubel Castle is made up of several connected features rather than one conventional building. The complex includes the Bottle House, a clock tower, a windmill, a blacksmith shop and a printing press. There is also a Santa Fe caboose on the property and the Tin Palace, a former packing house that became part of the Rubel family home.The clock tower is among the structures that give the site its castle-like appearance, while the towers and passages create an unusual arrangement that grew gradually rather than from a single architectural plan. The use of bottles and salvaged objects is also visible in the character of the buildings. As the historical society puts it, Rubel Castle was built around the remains of a former citrus-packing complex and reservoir, turning parts of an older Glendora landscape into something entirely different.The materials used at Rubel Castle were not simply convenient construction supplies. Many came from a period when Glendora was changing rapidly. Citrus farming had shaped the area, but orchards and agricultural structures were increasingly being replaced by suburban development. Buildings and equipment that had once been ordinary parts of local life were being demolished, abandoned or discarded.Rubel gathered some of those remnants and incorporated them into the castle. That gives the site a connection to the town beyond its unusual appearance. The castle became a place where materials and memories from the city’s agricultural past were given another purpose. What survived at Rubel Castle was therefore not just a collection of discarded objects, but pieces of an earlier Glendora embedded in a structure that continued to grow for decades.Today, the site is owned and operated by the Glendora Historical Society and can be visited only through scheduled tours. The castle remains a record of Rubel’s long building project, but also of the community that gathered around it. Friends, relatives, neighbours and the wider group known as the Pharmhands became part of its history. The result is a California castle assembled over years from concrete, bottles, metal, machinery and salvaged fragments, rather than a building transported from another place or period.
Article Summary: Michael Clarke Rubel began building Rubel Castle when he was just 19. He mixed concrete almost every day, adding towers, walls and other structures to the site. Much of what Rubel used had once been destined for demolition, abandonment or the scrap yard. Friends, neighbours and relatives helped with the physical work.

Article Title: In 2019, Florida began sinking mermaid-shaped reef sculptures; the project now has more than 300 habitat and art modules in South Florida
Article Text:
Florida began sinking mermaid-shaped reef sculptures

Combining art with reef restoration

Cities support artificial reef projects

More than 300 sculpted reef modules, including ocean-friendly concrete mermaids, now sit on the seafloor off South Florida as part of a growing marine restoration project launched seven years ago. Known as the 1000 Mermaids Artificial Reef Project, the initiative combines public art with habitat creation to help restore damaged marine ecosystems. According to records from Ocean Rescue Alliance International, the non-profit organisation leading the project, the team began placing the structures off Palm Beach County in 2019 and has since expanded south into Broward County. The project uses large reef modules made in partnership with Reef Cells, an engineering company based in Boynton Beach. Each module weighs between 2,200 and 5,500 pounds and is made from pH-neutral, environmentally friendly concrete designed to support marine life. The structures are not simply underwater artworks. They contain holes, textured surfaces and sheltered spaces where fish, lobsters and other marine animals can live and grow.To create the sculptures, artists make body casts of real people and use them to produce concrete mermaids, mermen and other ocean-themed figures.The sculptures are attached to heavy reef bases along with other modules designed specifically as fish habitats. The structures also use a patented system called Coral Lok. Developed by architectural sculptor and reef builder Chris O'Hare, the system uses specialised plugs that allow researchers and conservation workers to attach nursery-grown coral fragments directly to the artificial reefs. The system removes the need for underwater epoxy or other potentially harmful adhesives. "We focus all of our projects around the restoration of marine habitat," said Shelby Thomas, a marine biologist and founder of Ocean Rescue Alliance International, in an interview about the group's work. "When we create art projects, it is a small fraction art, and a majority is focused on habitat creation and marine resource restoration." Thomas said the artwork has a purpose beyond its appearance. It helps attract public interest and funding for marine conservation. "I ultimately started [ORAI] because I realized the biggest threat to humanity was the disconnection from nature. I knew from a social-physiological perspective we must create connection to have sustained change," Thomas said. "And so, I fell in love with art and its ability to connect people to the ocean and sustainably fund large-scale restoration."Local governments across South Florida have supported the artificial reefs as a way to encourage marine tourism while reducing pressure on fragile natural reefs. According to official documents from the City of Hollywood, its Community Redevelopment Agency worked with Ocean Rescue Alliance International to create a 20-module reef about one mile offshore in water 35 to 40 feet deep. The first installation included five types of art sculptures, including a mermaid tail that swimmers could pass through, a vintage diver suit module and several mermaid statues. After the deep-water project, the city expanded its work with the organisation to create sites closer to shore. The City's offshore reef guide describes the "Guardians of the Reef" installation, which was placed in water about 10 feet deep across four locations, including areas near North Beach Park, Harry Berry Park and Keating Park. Because the sites are shallow, snorkelers and other beachgoers can swim out from shore to see the sculptures. Visitors do not need charter boats or advanced diving equipment.The Florida Reef Tract stretches for more than 360 miles along Florida's southeastern coast and is the only barrier reef system in the continental United States. According to environmental information from Ocean Rescue Alliance International, the natural reef supports billions of dollars in economic activity each year through fishing and tourism. It also helps reduce wave energy by up to 97 per cent during major storms. However, the reef has suffered major damage from Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease, rising ocean temperatures and physical damage caused by human activity. Artificial reefs can help by giving recreational divers alternative sites to visit, reducing pressure on fragile natural coral areas. Over time, the concrete structures become covered with coralline algae, sponges and soft corals, gradually turning the sculptures into living marine communities. The 1000 Mermaids project continues to add new modules along Florida's coast, with more installations planned in international locations, including Mexico and the Caribbean.
Article Summary: The 1000 Mermaids Artificial Reef Project combines public art with habitat creation to help restore damaged marine ecosystems. The project uses large reef modules made in partnership with Reef Cells, an engineering company based in Boynton Beach. Each module weighs between 2,200 and 5,500 pounds and is made from pH-neutral, environmentally friendly concrete.

Article Title: In 2020, Phoenix coated 36 miles of roads to fight extreme heat; surfaces became 12°F cooler at noon, but heat exposure for pedestrians rose 5.5°F
Article Text:
Phoenix coated 36 miles of roads to fight extreme heat

Why the roads became cooler

The problem for pedestrians

What it means for city planning

Painting city streets with a light-coloured, reflective coating can cool the asphalt underneath, but it can also increase heat exposure for people walking on the road. That unexpected trade-off emerged from a major trial in the American Southwest. In 2020, the City of Phoenix Street Transportation Department coated 36 miles of neighbourhood roads and a public parking lot with CoolSeal, a grey, water-based asphalt treatment designed to reduce the urban heat island effect. Researchers from Arizona State University (ASU) studied the treated roads for a year. Their findings showed that while the coating successfully lowered road temperatures, it also created a more complicated situation for pedestrian comfort and safety.Traditional dark asphalt absorbs large amounts of sunlight and can reach temperatures of up to 180°F during the hottest summer periods. The roads also store heat and slowly release it after sunset, keeping urban areas warm through the night. To reduce this effect, Phoenix applied a reflective coating to selected residential streets across eight council districts. ASU researchers found that the treated roads were 2.4°F cooler at sunrise and 10.5 to 12°F cooler around midday.The coating also lowered temperatures below the road surface. Because the pavement reflected more sunlight instead of absorbing it, the treated roads stayed much cooler than older asphalt. City engineers also noted that lower temperatures below the surface could help roads last longer, potentially reducing maintenance costs over time.Despite the cooler pavement, researchers found an unexpected effect on people walking nearby. To understand how people actually experience outdoor heat, ASU researchers used a mobile weather station called "MaRTy". The equipment measures mean radiant temperature, which looks at the amount of heat radiation absorbed by the human body outdoors. The coating reflected sunlight away from the road, but the energy did not simply disappear. Much of the reflected heat moved sideways and upwards into the surrounding area, exposing pedestrians to more radiation. The ASU study found that the average mean radiant heat exposure for pedestrians increased by about 5.5°F on coated streets during the hottest part of the day. "Perhaps the most meaningful measurement is the mean radiant temperature," ASU scientist Ariane Middel said during the project.The Phoenix findings have attracted attention from urban planners as cities around the world look for ways to deal with rising temperatures. Similar projects in other cities, including Los Angeles, have found similar trade-offs, with cooler road surfaces but greater heat exposure for people at street level. Researchers say reflective road coatings should not be treated as a complete solution to extreme urban heat. Human comfort depends on more than the temperature of the pavement. Shade from trees, buildings and other structures can make a major difference. "If you're standing over one of these surfaces on a hot day, you're still going to be hot if you're not in the shade," said Jennifer Vanos, an associate professor in ASU's School of Sustainability who worked on the research. "So if we really want to be pushing towards true solutions to the heat problems, it's not going to be just paint all the streets white. You're going to have to really keep thinking about shade." Later phases of the Phoenix programme continued to test newer versions of the coating, including CoolSeal 2.0, while the city expanded its Cool Corridors Program. City officials are using the research to understand which neighbourhoods can benefit most from reflective materials. Open residential streets and parking areas with little natural shade may need additional measures, particularly trees and shade structures, to ensure that efforts to cool the pavement do not increase heat exposure for pedestrians.
Article Summary: Phoenix coated 36 miles of roads to fight extreme heat. Researchers found that the treated roads were 2.4°F cooler at sunrise and 10.5 to 12°F colder around midday. Researchers say reflective road coatings should not be treated as a complete solution to extreme urban heat.

Article Title: Alaska eradicated rats from a 6,869-acre Aleutian island more than two centuries after they arrived in a shipwreck; within two years some native bird populations had increased 200% or more and missing
Article Text:
Alaska eradicated rats from a 6,869-acre Aleutian island

Native birds make a rapid comeback

Island gets its traditional name back

More than two centuries after a shipwreck brought non-native rats to a remote Alaskan island, removing the invasive rodents has led to a rapid recovery of wildlife across the 6,869-acre island in the Aleutian archipelago. According to monitoring reports and press releases from the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the National Wildlife Refuge System, native bird populations on Hawadax Island increased by 200 per cent or more within just two years of the rat removal. Seabirds that had disappeared from the island have also started returning to its rocky cliffs to nest. The island, once known as Rat Island, got its invasive rat population around 1780 after a Japanese ship ran aground on its coast. The surviving Norway rats (Rattus norvegicus) multiplied and began feeding on bird eggs, chicks and adult birds.Native island species had evolved without land-based mammalian predators. As a result, ground-nesting and burrowing birds had few defences against the rats. Their populations fell sharply as the infestation spread across the island. In autumn 2008, the USFWS worked with conservation groups, including The Nature Conservancy and Island Conservation, to begin a major rat eradication campaign across the 10-square-mile island.Specialist teams used helicopters to spread rodenticide bait across the island according to a carefully planned digital grid. The operation successfully removed the rats. After several years of monitoring to confirm that no rodents had survived, the USFWS officially declared the island rat-free.Wildlife surveys after the eradication showed quick changes among ground-nesting and shorebird populations. Glaucous-winged gulls, song sparrows, rock sandpipers and black oystercatchers all increased in number. Biologists recorded a three-fold increase in glaucous-winged gull nests within two years of the operation. Surveys also found nesting tufted puffins and storm-petrels returning to the island. These birds had been almost completely wiped out during the years of rat infestation. Stacey Buckelew of Island Conservation described the dramatic change she saw after the rats were removed. “When I first landed on what was Rat Island in 2007, it was an eerily silent place,” Buckelew said in statements recorded by the USFWS. “A typical Aleutian island is teeming with wildlife, swirling with noisy, pungent birds. Not this place. It was crisscrossed with rat trails, littered with rat scat, scavenged bird bones, it even smelled…” During later monitoring visits, Buckelew said the island was “hardly recognizable among the cacophony of birds calling everywhere; it's alive with bird fledglings”. “The return of bird life to Hawadax Island is an inspiring example of what we can accomplish when we work together to fix a longstanding problem,” Randy Hagenstein, Alaska state director for The Nature Conservancy, said in USFWS press materials.The ecological recovery also led to the island getting back its traditional name. In May 2012, after a proposal from the Aleutian Pribilof Islands Association, the U.S. Board on Geographic Names officially changed the name from Rat Island back to Hawadax Island. The Unangam Tunuu (Aleut) word Hawadax roughly means "entry" or "welcome". Long-term research published in scientific journals, including Nature Scientific Reports, has shown that removing the rats helped restore wider natural processes on the island. As bird populations returned, they helped restore the natural balance of the island's intertidal ecosystem. Birds also brought marine nutrients onto land through their droppings, enriching the soil and helping native plants recover. Gregg Howald, North America Region Director for Island Conservation, said the project demonstrated how effective partnerships can restore damaged ecosystems. “Hawadax Island is on a trajectory for recovery and the ecological gains we are witnessing are tremendous,” Howald said in USFWS reports. “They are a sustained testament to a conservation methodology and partnership that works.” Today, Hawadax Island is part of the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge. Its successful recovery has also made it an important example for future projects aimed at removing invasive predators from islands around the world.
Article Summary: Hawadax Island, in the Aleutian archipelago, was infested with Norway rats around 1780 after a Japanese ship ran aground on its coast. The rats multiplied and began feeding on bird eggs, chicks and adult birds. In 2008, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service began a major rat eradication campaign across the 10-square-mile island. Biologists recorded a three-fold increase in glaucous- winged gull nests within two years of the operation.

Article Title: In 2021, Alabama students began placing discarded Christmas trees along Gulf Coast dunes to trap sand; each year about 200 students now add roughly 3,000 native plants around them
Article Text:
Discarded Christmas trees

How Christmas trees help build dunes

Students and community work together

Helping the Gulf Coast recover

Discarded holiday trees collected from living rooms across Alabama are finding a second life along the Gulf of Mexico, forming the foundation of a student-led coastal restoration campaign. Discarded Christmas trees collected from homes across Alabama are getting a second life along the Gulf of Mexico, helping form the base of a student-led coastal restoration project. What began in 2021 as a small environmental effort has grown into an annual project on Alabama’s public beaches. Each year, around 200 high school students and community volunteers gather along the shoreline in Gulf Shores to place recycled Christmas trees and plant thousands of native plants to strengthen fragile sand dunes.According to public records from the City of Gulf Shores and historical information maintained by coastal restoration company Dune Doctors, the project combines sand trapping with native plant planting. Recycled Christmas trees are placed and secured in selected areas of the beach where wind-blown sand naturally collects around their branches. Over time, the trapped sand builds up and forms the base of new dunes.To help hold the sand in place during storms and strong winds, students plant about 3,000 native coastal plants around the tree barriers each year. These include sea oats (Uniola paniculata) and panicgrass (Panicum amarum).Sand dunes act as an important natural barrier that protects roads, buildings and inland habitats from storm tides and coastal erosion. When strong winds blow across the beach, loose sand is carried along until it hits an obstacle. By placing used Christmas trees in lines along or across the beach, volunteers create simple barriers that slow the wind. As the wind moves through the branches and needles, its speed drops and sand falls around the trees. Over several months, the sand can completely cover the branches. The trees provide an immediate structure, but the new sand mounds can still be damaged by wind if they are not planted with vegetation. Native plants provide longer-term protection. Sea oats, for example, develop deep, spreading root systems that hold sand together. As the plants grow, they help turn loose sand into a more stable dune that can continue to protect the coastline.The annual restoration effort depends on cooperation between local government, schools and environmental groups. The City of Gulf Shores operates public collection points after the holiday season, allowing residents to donate Christmas trees that are clean and free of decorations. Without the programme, many of these trees could end up in local landfills. City crews then move the collected trees to selected beach access points. Student groups are given instructions on coastal ecology and how to place the trees and plant vegetation. "Our goal is to give students a hands-on experience in environmental stewardship while actively protecting our coastal infrastructure," event organisers said in project briefs published on the City of Gulf Shores civic portal. "Seeing how a discarded household item can directly help rebuild our beach ecosystem gives these young people a lasting sense of ownership over their local environment." Timeline records from Dune Doctors, a coastal restoration company involved in beach management projects in the region, say the use of student volunteers has helped reduce the cost of manual dune planting while also speeding up habitat recovery after major storms.The combination of recycled trees and native plants is aimed at a major problem along the Gulf Coast, where hurricanes and powerful winter storms can quickly strip away beaches and dunes. Dunes without vegetation can lose several metres of height during a single major storm. Dunes supported by strong root systems are generally better able to withstand storm surges and waves. The old Christmas trees can also add organic material to the beach. As they break down, they release nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus into the normally nutrient-poor sand. This can help young sea oat plants develop roots more quickly. The plants also provide important habitat for wildlife. Project managers say sea oats and panicgrass can create nesting and shelter areas for animals such as the endangered Alabama beach mouse (Peromyscus polionotus ammobates) and several species of shorebirds that use vegetated dunes for protection from predators and severe weather. With hundreds of students taking part each year, the programme has developed into a simple, low-cost way for communities to reuse an everyday holiday item while helping protect Alabama’s coastline.
Article Summary: Around 200 high school students and community volunteers gather along the shoreline in Gulf Shores to place recycled Christmas trees and plant thousands of native plants to strengthen fragile sand dunes. Recycled Christmas trees are placed and secured in selected areas of the beach where wind-blown sand naturally collects around their branches.

Article Title: MAGA skids on maple syrup: US-Canada ties on a slippery slope
Article Text:
Carney claimed that Trump’s demands are reaching beyond tariffs into the country’s national identity and sovereignty. (AP Photo)

TOI correspondent From Washington:

Canada has long been seen as America’s best friend, even sibling: close enough to borrow sugar (or maple syrup) from, harmless enough to tease with quips like how the country is like a loft apartment over a great party (Robin Williams) and “I don’t even know what street Canada is on” (Al Capone). Even a looming trade war did not dull the humour.Now, Prime Minister Mark Carney says US President Donald Trump is embarking on something rather more serious and provocative than demanding better access for American dairy farmers: he wants to change Canada culturally and linguistically.Invoking Quebec, the most distinctly French-speaking part of Canada, Carney on Saturday made the astonishing claim that Trump’s demands are reaching beyond tariffs into the country’s national identity and sovereignty.“We were ready and close to having a comprehensive agreement that would be fair to both countries. But they made changes, including threats on the French language and Quebec culture and Canadian culture. That is not acceptable,” Carney said in remarks that revealed the trade war between the two countries is no longer merely a fight over who pays more for cheese; it is becoming a quarrel over what it means to be Canadian.It is quite a transformation for two countries whose economies are so intertwined that distinguishing where an American product ends and a Canadian one begins can require the services of a forensic accountant. The latest escalation arrived Saturday, when Trump imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian imports. Canada responded with the economic equivalent of saying, If you insist on bringing a knife to dinner, we have cutlery too, promising a “dollar-for-dollar” retaliation from September 8 targeting American steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment and other goods.The damage is fairly modest because the new American tariffs cover only about 5% of Canadian exports to the US -- small beer in a $900-billion per year trade relationship. But the psychological bill is immense.For generations, Americans have treated Canada as the reassuringly sensible friend or sibling — the place where people speak English, French and, apparently, apologize in both languages. The stereotypical American view has been that Canadians are essentially Americans who say “sorry” more often. Not anymore; Trump’s “51st state” rhetoric has helped turn that gentle stereotype upside down. Carney is now arguing that Canada must no longer assume geography automatically guarantees prosperity and security. Earlier this year he called the changing international order a “rupture, not a transition.”That fissure has nudged Ottawa toward an unlikely strategic thought: perhaps Canada should diversify away from its giant southern neighbor.Carney has already pursued a cautious rapprochement with Beijing. During his January visit to China, Canada and China reached an initial tariff arrangement under which Ottawa agreed to reduce tariffs on a capped number of Chinese electric vehicles while Beijing lowered duties on Canadian canola and eased restrictions on other agricultural exports. Some American strategists worry that a Canada increasingly alienated from the US could become a more attractive economic partner for China — particularly in agriculture, minerals, energy, electric vehicles and infrastructure. Beijing would gain not so much a “foothold” in North America overnight as something potentially more valuable: a door previously assumed to be firmly inside Washington’s house.Still, Canada is unlikely to trade Uncle Sam for Uncle Xi because Ottawa remains deeply integrated with the US economy and security system.
