But Carney’s China policy suggests that Trump’s America-first strategy may be teaching Ottawa -- like much of the world is also learning -- the oldest lesson in international economics: when your biggest customer starts charging you for friendship, it is probably time to look for other customers.Not that all this is worrying Trump. “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!! They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!’ he huffed on Truth Social on Sunday as the wheels started coming off what has long been one of the most comfortable and uncomplicated bilateral relationships in the world.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump is embarking on something rather more serious and provocative than demanding better access for American dairy farmers: he wants to change Canada culturally and linguistically. Canada responded with the economic equivalent of saying, If you insist on bringing a knife to dinner, we have cutlery too, promising a “dollar-for-dollar” retaliation.

Article Title: Ohio mother was in Costa Rica when 18-year-old son died in car crash; hospital never contacted her, she later learned his body parts were removed as 'anatomical gifts' without consent
Article Text:
Andrea Mauk with her son Damon and husband Edward. (Photo: Andrea Mauk)

A mother left grieving from another country

'A call to me was all I wanted'

Andrea Mauk says she was never contacted before tissues, including her son Damon’s eyes, were recovered after his death. Now, she is campaigning for stronger safeguards around tissue donation and family consent. (Photo: Andrea Mauk)

Her grief became a campaign for change

Organ donation system faces wider scrutiny

'Damon deserved to have dignity in death'

For Andrea Mauk, the phone call telling her that her 18-year-old son Damon had died was already a moment no mother should ever have to endure. But while she was thousands of miles away in Costa Rica, grieving a son she could not reach, another decision was being made about his body.When Mauk finally returned home, she says she learned that parts of Damon's body had been removed as "anatomical gifts" without her knowledge or consent."I was completely devastated," Mauk, 42, told The New York Post. "I went to the funeral home and couldn't even look at him after they'd taken pieces of his body. They stole my son's eyes. I didn't want to remember Damon like that."Damon had only just graduated from high school. He was studying for his real-estate license and, according to his mother, was at a stage in life where his future was beginning to take shape.On June 24, 2023, his car reportedly slid off a rural road in Lucas, Ohio, and crashed into a tree. Mauk was in Costa Rica with her husband and friends when her parents gave her the devastating news."They had to sedate me," she recalled.What has haunted Mauk ever since, she says, is that the hospital never called her. She was listed as Damon's primary emergency contact, and she says her phone number was readily available in his records.Damon was not a registered organ donor.Yet, according to Mauk, consent for tissue donation was obtained from his biological father, a man she says had played little role in their son's life.Mauk says she was not opposed to donation itself. What devastated her was being excluded from the decision at the moment she was losing her son.She later learned that Damon's eyes, skin, heart valves, ligaments and other tissues had been recovered as "anatomical gifts." Some of the tissue, she says, was subsequently sent to research or biologics organizations, while his eyes were sent to Argentina.For a mother who says she had been deeply involved in her son's life, the experience left her feeling powerless."I loved Damon very deeply," she said. "I had him when I was very young and we always joked that we brought each other up. We were incredibly close."Then came the words that perhaps best capture what she believes could have changed everything: "A call to me was all I wanted."Mauk says she does not want Damon's story to be interpreted as an argument against organ or tissue donation. Instead, she wants families to have a stronger voice and hospitals to follow clearer procedures when a potential donor dies.Her personal loss eventually turned into advocacy. Mauk contacted lawmakers and testified before the Ohio Senate about what she believes are gaps in the law. She also launched a Change.org petition calling for "Damon's Law", which seeks stronger safeguards around tissue donation and family notification."I believe in organ donation," Mauk said. "This is not about ending the gift of life."For her, the issue is about consent, communication and dignity — particularly for families confronting an unexpected death.Mauk's campaign comes at a time when the US organ procurement system is facing increased federal scrutiny.On July 21, the US Department of Health and Human Services, under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., announced an initiative to reform the organ transplant system and establish clearer, enforceable policies concerning donor eligibility.The move followed an investigation into a major organ procurement organization serving Kentucky, Ohio and West Virginia. Investigators raised concerns about cases in which patients may not have been deceased when procurement procedures began, as well as neurological assessments, coordination with medical teams and consent practices.Organ and tissue donation in the US is governed by a combination of federal and state regulations. Hospitals participating in Medicare or Medicaid are required to notify organ procurement organizations of deaths and imminent deaths, even when a patient is not a registered donor.OPOs are then responsible for approaching families of potential donors. The system has faced criticism over how families are contacted and how consent discussions are handled.For Mauk, the debate over organ donation is inseparable from the memory of her son.She says Damon was more than a potential donor. He was the boy she raised, the young man whose future she watched unfold and someone she describes as the "light of her life."Her fight is now about making sure other families do not experience what she says she went through."Damon deserved to have dignity in death," Mauk said.And every appeal she makes carries the same deeply personal sign-off:"Forever Damon's mother."
Article Summary: Andrea Mauk says she was never contacted before tissues, including her son Damon’s eyes, were recovered after his death. Now, she is campaigning for stronger safeguards around tissue donation and family consent. Her campaign comes at a time when the US organ procurement system is facing increased federal scrutiny.

Article Title: A Detroit couple bought a vacant 1925 bank and neighboring bar for $66,000; 13 years later, one old bank vault is a den and another is a wine cellar
Article Text:
Michael and Lynne carried out much of the renovation themselves. (Pictures: Homes.com)

From abandoned bank to family home

The former People’s State Bank had already gone through several changes before the couple bought it.

Copper entrance survived decline

More than a renovation project

A former bank building in Detroit, Michigan that sat vacant for about a decade has been turned into a two-bedroom home after a couple spent years restoring it by hand. The unusual property, built in 1925, is now on the market for $1.3 million.Lynne Savino and her husband, Michael, bought the abandoned building in 2013 through an estate sale, according to Homes.com. The purchase price was $66,000 and included the neighbouring property, a former bar at 3415 Michigan Ave. The couple had sold their home in Detroit’s Green Acres area to fund the purchase and the work that followed.The former People’s State Bank had already gone through several changes before the couple bought it. It was later used as an after-hours club, and the building had suffered from scrapping and graffiti. Still, Savino saw potential in the structure and wanted to turn it into a home.The renovation became a major project. The couple moved into the building in May 2014, even though much of the house was still under construction. At first, there was no kitchen, laundry room or shower. Savino placed her bed in the middle of the construction area and gradually worked on different parts of the property.“I did not have a shower for a month. I didn’t have a laundry room for two months, and I didn’t have a kitchen until September,” Savino said. During that time, she traded cooking meals and bottles of wine with friends in exchange for using their showers and washing machines.Savino said she was drawn to the building because of its size, light and unusual features. The property had half-round windows at the top, allowing sunlight to enter the space.“I thought it was fantastic. The sunlight would be pouring through the half-round windows at the top, and I had two cats at the time, and it was just heavenly,” she said.Michael, who worked as a cement contractor, and Lynne carried out much of the renovation themselves. They kept the building’s exterior largely unchanged, apart from installing a new roof. The couple had considered several other unusual buildings before settling on this one.The bank had been built with an open floor plan. It included a main-level vault, an employee bathroom and another vault in the basement. By the time the Savinos bought the building, the vault doors were gone. Radiators had also been removed, which Savino believed was the work of scrappers.The basement vault was eventually converted into a wine cellar. The couple also added a loft, which became the location of the primary bedroom and a second bathroom. The space had previously been used as a DJ booth when the building operated as a club. To work out the layout of the loft, Savino used newspaper taped to the floor to mark the planned spaces.The finished property now has two bedrooms and two bathrooms. It covers about 3,000 square feet and is located in West Corktown, one of Detroit’s oldest areas. Listing agent Endrina Halili Malkowski of Keller Williams Legacy described it as a highly unusual residential conversion. “It is the most unique building that’s been renovated completely and being used as a residential building currently,” she said.One of the features that survived the building’s years of neglect was a large copper vestibule at the entrance. The former after-hours club had painted over the entrance, which helped keep the copper hidden from people stripping the building for valuable materials. Savino later removed the paint herself.“I call it my $30,000 vestibule because copper is expensive,” she said. She used nut picks to work through the detailed sections of the vestibule and remove the paint.The couple also retained several other traces of the building’s past. Original marble windowsills remain in the home, and some have engraved signatures left by former partygoers or people who entered the abandoned building.The basement still has spray paint and handwritten markings on its walls, connecting the finished residence to the building’s earlier years.The Savinos also added modern features while keeping those older details. The home has a 20-foot-long kitchen island and a custom mural of a koi fish painted by local artist Phybr. Phybr also painted murals on the exterior of the neighbouring Airbnb property and on a storage container in the backyard. The container once held all of the Savinos’ belongings while the renovation was under way and is included in the sale of the home.The unusual property eventually became part of Savino’s cooking class business. It was also used as an event venue. The home has hosted different gatherings, including a wedding reception for a friend who worked for the city of Detroit.For Savino, using the house for these activities was a natural extension of what she had imagined when she first bought the building. “From the beginning, I always told my husband that it’s a space that should be shared. It’s big, it’s cool, it’s a great Detroit story,” she said.The couple’s former bar next door was also given a new use. According to the report, the property has been used as an Airbnb with three loft apartments and is separately listed for $485,000. The two properties can also be sold together.The former bank itself is now listed for $1.3 million. The average house price in southwest Detroit at $124,480, with an average price of $110 per square foot. The Savinos’ property is listed at about $433 per square foot.
Article Summary: The former People’s State Bank had already gone through several changes before the couple bought it. It was later used as an after-hours club, and the building had suffered from scrapping and graffiti. The couple moved into the building in May 2014, even though much of the house was still under construction.

Article Title: In 1967, Henry Pigott sold his North Carolina island home to help create Cape Lookout National Seashore; a life estate let him stay until his death as Portsmouth Village's last male resident
Article Text:
Portsmouth Island

Life estate allowed Pigott to stay

Historic village preserved

When the federal government began bringing the windswept barrier islands of eastern North Carolina under protected parkland, a quiet property deal near Pamlico Sound helped bring the story of a once-thriving coastal community to an end. In 1967, Henry Pigott agreed to sell his property on Portsmouth Island to help create Cape Lookout National Seashore. As part of the deal, he received a life estate, allowing him to remain in his ancestral home for the rest of his life. The land purchase, recorded in historical narration scripts and administrative records published by the National Park Service (NPS), marked an important step in creating the national seashore. It also made Pigott the last male resident of Portsmouth Village, an isolated 18th-century settlement that was already slowly disappearing.Portsmouth Village was established by the North Carolina Colonial Assembly in 1753 as an important "lightering" port. Heavy ocean-going ships would unload their cargo onto smaller, shallow-draft boats, which could then move through the dangerous inlets of Pamlico Sound.By 1860, the village had grown to nearly 700 residents. But the opening of deeper inlets nearby, powerful hurricanes and changing trade routes led to a steady decline during the 20th century. The closure of the local United States Life-Saving Station in 1937 and the post office in 1959 further weakened the island's connection to the mainland economy. By the mid-1960s, only a small number of elderly residents were left on the roadless island. One of them was Pigott, a Black mail carrier, guide and craftsman who was born there in 1896. His grandmother had lived on the island during slavery, and Pigott spent his entire life closely connected to the village and its people.When federal agencies began buying property across the Core Banks to create Cape Lookout National Seashore, Pigott agreed to sell his 1902 yellow wooden house while keeping the right to live there for the rest of his life. The arrangement allowed the government to acquire the land for conservation while ensuring that long-time residents were not forced to leave their homes. NPS records show that Pigott remained an important part of the shrinking community during his final years. He looked after his home, carried mail and supplies across the water, helped hunters, carved waterfowl decoys and checked on the village's only other full-time residents, Marian Gray Babb and Elma Dixon. Historical records compiled by the Friends of Portsmouth Island and the NPS say Pigott died in January 1971. His death brought permanent life in the historic settlement to an end. Without Pigott there to support them, the two remaining women left for the mainland later that year. Portsmouth Village was left completely empty for the first time in more than 200 years.After the island was fully depopulated, the 250-acre Portsmouth Village historic district was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1978. The National Park Service later preserved more than 20 historic buildings, turning the abandoned village into a living museum of coastal and maritime history. The Henry Pigott House remains one of the main historic sites in the village. Through preservation work by the National Park Service and the Friends of Portsmouth Island volunteer organisation, the house has been repaired, protected from the weather and furnished with period-appropriate objects. Inside, visitors can see original belongings that belonged to Pigott and his sisters. Exhibits also explain his role as the village's final male resident.The house has faced damage from major storms over the years. Hurricane Dorian in 2019, for example, caused serious interior damage. Cleanup work and window replacement projects helped protect the building and allowed it to continue serving as an educational site for visitors arriving by ferry or private boat. Today, Portsmouth Village can only be reached by water and remains part of the wider Cape Lookout National Seashore. Its quiet roads and preserved buildings offer a physical reminder of the barrier island communities that once shaped the Outer Banks before population decline, changing trade and conservation transformed the landscape. Pigott's decision to sell his home while keeping the right to live there also became part of that history. His death marked the final chapter of permanent settlement in a village that had survived for more than two centuries.
Article Summary: Portsmouth Village was established by the North Carolina Colonial Assembly in 1753 as an important "lightering" port. By 1860, the village had grown to nearly 700 residents. But the opening of deeper inlets nearby, powerful hurricanes and changing trade routes led to a steady decline during the 20th century. The 250-acre Portsmouth Village historic district was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1978.

Article Title: Texas police sergeant accused of using Flock cameras to stalk female coworker; he surrendered his law-enforcement licence and avoided prosecution
Article Text:
Flock Safety ALPR camera system on a roadside pole

System flags unusual searches

Criminal and administrative investigations

Questions over police surveillance technology

A former Texas police officer accused of using automated licence-plate reader technology to monitor a female colleague has surrendered his law-enforcement licence to avoid criminal charges. Michael Palitz, who previously served as a sergeant with the Pasadena Police Department in the Greater Houston area, reached an agreement with local prosecutors after an internal investigation into the alleged misuse of police surveillance systems. According to an investigation by the Houston Chronicle, along with reports from FOX 26 Houston and KPRC 2, Palitz left his position after automated security systems used by the police department detected unusual activity.The surveillance technology involved was supplied by Flock Safety, a company that operates networks of licence-plate reading cameras designed to record vehicle movements on public roads. Police departments across the US use the cameras to help find stolen vehicles, locate missing people and collect evidence in criminal investigations. The system flagged Palitz’s account after detecting an unusually large number of searches involving one particular vehicle.Pasadena City Council Member Emmanuel Guerrero described the allegations that emerged during the internal investigation. "Based on what we gathered, [he] was using our camera system, our Flock system, to track and stalk a female officer," Guerrero said. Guerrero said the system's security features helped identify the unusual activity. "My understanding of the investigation, he would use it to specifically track another female officer, and the system, after so much usage, pinged his specific account, raising a red flag," Guerrero told FOX 26 Houston.After the searches were discovered, city officials launched both administrative and criminal investigations. Information released by the police department showed that the case involved separate allegations made by two employees against each other. Both employees resigned from the Pasadena Police Department before the administrative investigations were completed. Under Texas law, police administrative investigations remain confidential when an officer resigns before the process is formally concluded. As a result, no official disciplinary action was recorded in the administrative case. The criminal investigations were sent to the Harris County District Attorney’s Office for review. Prosecutors decided not to bring charges over one set of allegations. In the case involving the alleged improper surveillance of the female officer, prosecutors agreed to drop the criminal proceedings on the condition that Palitz surrender his law-enforcement credentials. The Pasadena Police Department confirmed the outcome in an official statement. "In one matter, the District Attorney's Office declined prosecution," the department stated. "In the other, the matter was resolved through and agreement requiring the individual to surrender his Texas Commission on Law Enforcement (TCOLE) peace officer license in lieu of criminal prosecution". The department said it would not make further comments because both the internal and criminal investigations had ended and neither person was still employed by the city.The Pasadena case has raised concerns about how law-enforcement agencies control access to surveillance technology. Cities across Texas have increasingly turned to automated camera networks, leading to questions about who can access the systems and how their use is monitored. Civil liberties experts and legal commentators said that while software can detect unusual or unauthorised searches, departments must still ensure officers are held accountable when technology is misused. James Henderson, executive director of the Texas Civil Rights Project, discussed the wider concerns surrounding surveillance technology in comments cited by KPRC 2. "When an officer allegedly misuses a surveillance tool, it in its very nature raises a public trust question," Henderson said. "People need confidence that the system designed to protect the community cannot at the same time be used to improperly monitor, intimidate or intrude upon private citizens".Henderson said public confidence depends largely on how police departments control and use powerful surveillance tools. "The bigger issue is not necessarily whether police have technology, but it's really shrouded in whether or not police departments have earned the public's trust to use this technology responsibly," Henderson added. During the early stages of the investigation, Pasadena Mayor Thomas Schoenbein said the city remained committed to maintaining high standards within its police department. "We are committed to maintaining the integrity of our organization and the confidence our residents place in us," Schoenbein said. "As such, the City of Pasadena stands with our dedicated police officers who work every day to uphold the highest standards and keep our community safe". Palitz has now officially surrendered his law-enforcement licence to the Texas Commission on Law Enforcement. As a result, he is permanently barred from working as a sworn peace officer in Texas.
Article Summary: Michael Palitz was a sergeant with the Pasadena Police Department in the Greater Houston area. He was accused of using automated licence-plate reader technology to monitor a female colleague. Palitz surrendered his law-enforcement licence to the Texas Commission on Law Enforcement to avoid criminal charges.

Article Title: Four children forced to live in semitruck cab for nearly 7 years; US couple arrested for alleged neglect
Article Text:
Keisha Monique Epps, 51, a truck driver, and her fiancé, Tamra Stewart.

Four children allegedly lived inside the cab of a semitruck since December 2019 while their guardian drove routes between Atlanta and Miami, according to court documents. They were reportedly rarely allowed outside, attended no school for years and received little or no medical care.According to Fox News, Keisha Monique Epps, 51, a truck driver, and her fiancé, Tamra Stewart, 37, both from Georgia, were arrested in Jacksonville on August 6 following a multi-jurisdictional investigation.Epps faces four counts of child neglect, while Stewart also faces a capital sexual battery charge.Investigators said the children had been living in the truck since December 2019, spending "the majority of their days" inside the cab. They reportedly shared a single bunk, having to sleep curled up side by side because there was not enough room to lie flat.The children told investigators they were rarely allowed out of the truck, including to shower, use the restroom or exercise.A detective reportedly noticed that they were walking with an unnatural gait, which investigators attributed to years of confinement.The children also told authorities they had not attended a recognised school for several years.According to court documents, their last confirmed enrolment was in November 2020, after which they were allegedly directed to use an app that was not recognised as an accredited educational institution.The children were also allegedly denied medical and dental care. In one incident, a child reportedly suffered a severe burn from cooked noodles. Despite heavy bleeding, the child said she was not taken for medical treatment and was left with a permanent scar.Investigators further alleged that Stewart sexually abused the children and physically assaulted them when they confronted him about the abuse. The children said Epps was aware of the alleged abuse but continued to leave them alone with Stewart.One child was also found to have an untreated sexually transmitted infection, according to the arrest records.All information identifying the children, including their ages, sexes and relationships to Epps and Stewart, was redacted from the court documents.Epps and Stewart were being held at the Duval County Jail. Epps' bond was set at $400,012, while Stewart was being held without bond.Authorities said each of the four child-neglect counts against Epps carries a potential sentence of up to five years in prison, five years of probation and a fine of up to $5,000.
Article Summary: Keisha Monique Epps, 51, a truck driver, and her fiancé, Tamra Stewart, 37, both from Georgia, were arrested in Jacksonville on August 6 following a multi- jurisdictional investigation. Epps faces four counts of child neglect, while Stewart also faces a capital sexual battery charge. The children told investigators they were rarely allowed out of the truck, including to shower, use the restroom or exercise. They also told authorities they had not attended a recognised school for several years.

Article Title: 50 years ago, this California sanctuary began saving some of the world’s rarest gibbons, today, their morning songs are a remarkable story of survival
Article Text:
Gibbon Conservation Center director Gabi Skollar feeds one of the little apes

Caring for endangered gibbons

Research and education

Every morning, as dawn breaks over the dry hills north of Los Angeles, a chorus of sirens, deep hoots and high-pitched calls echoes across the Santa Clarita Valley. The sounds come from the Gibbon Conservation Center, a sanctuary that has spent half a century protecting some of the world’s most endangered primates. Founded in 1976, the sanctuary now houses around 40 gibbons belonging to five species, according to The Independent. Known for their complex vocal duets, these small apes are native to the tropical rainforests of Southeast Asia. Their numbers in the wild have fallen sharply because of deforestation, habitat loss and the illegal pet trade. For some of the species at the centre, fewer than 2,000 animals remain in the wild. The sanctuary was founded by the late Alan Mootnick, a self-taught primatologist who ran a home painting and remodelling business. Mootnick got his first gibbon, Spanky, in 1976 after responding to a newspaper advert. Although he had no formal degree in biology, he bought the 10-acre property in 1980 using money from his business and gradually turned it into a major centre for gibbon research and conservation.Over the years, Mootnick published scientific papers, welcomed researchers from around the world and helped experts identify different gibbon species.After Mootnick died in 2011 from complications following surgery, the centre came under the leadership of director Gabi Skollar. Skollar moved from Hungary to the US in 2005 to study under Mootnick. She had planned to leave after finishing her studies but decided to stay and run the facility. “We have to keep going and take care of this place,” she said. Skollar now lives at the centre and manages its daily work with a team of animal care staff.The sanctuary works to maintain genetic diversity by carefully managing breeding programmes and exchanging animals with accredited zoos and other conservation facilities. One of its biggest achievements was becoming the first facility to successfully breed the endangered Javan gibbon in captivity. The species is native to Java, Indonesia. The centre is also preparing to send a pair of northern white-cheeked gibbons to the Pittsburgh Zoo as part of wider conservation efforts. Daily care requires carefully planned diets and, when needed, hand-rearing young animals. Caretaker Jodi Kleier prepares meals that include washed lettuce, steamed sweet potatoes and chopped bananas. Kleier also hand-reared a young gibbon named Rocky after his mother abandoned him at birth. Such cases can sometimes happen with first-time primate mothers. The gibbons also have their own personalities and vocal habits. A young northern white-cheeked gibbon named Pepper often starts the morning calls. A pileated gibbon named Violet joins in with her partner, Truman. Another resident, Pierre, has developed a particular dislike of male visitors and makes his feelings known through his calls.The centre is not only a home for endangered animals. It also serves as a place for non-invasive scientific research. Skollar is working towards a doctorate at the University of California, Los Angeles, studying gibbon vocalisation patterns. “There’s a lot of things that we can learn in a captive setting that can be shared with conservationists in the field and also with people working in sanctuaries rescuing gibbons,” Skollar said. The sanctuary also works with educational institutions, including The Teaching Zoo at Moorpark College. Every year, first-year college students visit the centre to learn about caring for exotic animals. Some later return to work at the sanctuary. Mara Rodriguez, a development coordinator at the Moorpark College zoo who first visited the centre in the 1990s, said the experience can change how people see the animals. “When I went out there for the first time in the 1990s, I didn't know what a gibbon was,” Rodriguez said. “Now I've raised four gibbons in my career.” She said visitors “will leave with a lasting impression and begin to care about the species”.Animal care specialist Sophia Paden also stressed that gibbons are highly social animals and should never be kept as pets. “Gibbons are a lot like us humans; they actually live in family groups,” Paden said in an interview with local media. “No primate should ever be a pet. Their needs are too complicated, and they pose a danger to people.” The sanctuary offers limited public tours on weekends, while schools and community groups regularly request educational visits. Looking ahead, the centre hopes to raise more money to build larger enclosures for the animals and create a permanent education centre on its 10-acre property. After 50 years of work, its goal remains the same: protecting gibbons, studying them and helping more people understand why these endangered apes need to survive in the wild.
Article Summary: Gibbon Conservation Center was founded in 1976 by Alan Mootnick. The sanctuary now houses around 40 gibbons belonging to five species. Gibbons are native to the tropical rainforests of Southeast Asia. Their numbers in the wild have fallen sharply because of deforestation, habitat loss and the illegal pet trade.

Article Title: Massive Burmese python seized at Coney Island after man showed illegal pet snake to crowd
Article Text:
Image: NYSDEC​

Man displayed a massive Burmese python to a crowd on the Coney Island boardwalk

Why Burmese pythons are illegal to own in New York

The python’s size was not disclosed

A crowded summer scene on New York’s Coney Island boardwalk took an unexpected turn when an environmental conservation police officer spotted a man showing off two snakes to a group of people, including children. The encounter happened on July 12 near the Riegelmann Boardwalk, where the larger of the two reptiles was identified by its owner as a Burmese python. The snake was not simply an unusual attraction for passers-by: keeping a Burmese python as a pet is illegal in New York state. The officer issued the man a ticket and confiscated the snake, which was later taken to the Nassau County Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals for care. State officials did not disclose the python’s length, although photographs showed two officers handling the large snake. The incident also highlighted why authorities restrict ownership of the species, which can pose risks to people and potentially harm native wildlife if released.The unusual encounter unfolded while the environmental conservation police officer was near the Riegelmann Boardwalk. State officials told CBS New York that roughly a dozen people had gathered around the man, with children among those watching him display the reptiles.One of the snakes was a ball python, which the man had around his neck. When the officer asked about the animals, the man said the second and larger snake was a Burmese python that he owned. That admission immediately raised a legal issue because Burmese pythons cannot legally be kept as pets in New York state. Rather than allowing the display to continue, the officer confiscated the Burmese python and issued the man a ticket. The snake was subsequently transported to the Nassau County Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, where it could be cared for after being removed from its owner.Burmese pythons are among the world's largest snakes and can grow to enormous sizes. Their ability to prey on a wide range of animals is also why authorities are concerned about what could happen if one escaped or was deliberately released. New York state officials cited the potential danger to people as well as the species’ ability to severely affect native wildlife populations if Burmese pythons are released. An established population of a large non-native predator could put additional pressure on native animals that have not evolved alongside it. The Coney Island incident therefore involved more than an unusual encounter between a snake owner and curious beachgoers. The presence of a prohibited species in a busy public area raised both legal and environmental concerns.Despite the snake being described as large, officials did not provide its exact length. Photographs released after the seizure showed two officers handling the Burmese python, giving an indication of the animal’s substantial size. The case also came as authorities were dealing with another Burmese python found elsewhere in the region. A separate eight-foot-long Burmese python was recently captured in Freehold, New Jersey, and officials believed that animal had been kept as a pet before being deliberately released. The Coney Island seizure serves as a reminder of the risks surrounding exotic pets that can eventually become difficult or dangerous to manage. What began as a snake being displayed to curious visitors on one of New York’s busiest waterfronts ended with the animal confiscated and placed in professional care.
Article Summary: An environmental conservation police officer spotted a man showing off two snakes to a group of people, including children. The larger of the two reptiles was identified by its owner as a Burmese python. The officer issued the man a ticket and confiscated the snake, which was later taken to the Nassau County Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals for care.

Article Title: In 2021, Johnston Atoll eradicated invasive yellow crazy ants after an 11-year effort; the refuge is home to nearly 13,000 red-tailed tropicbird nesting pairs
Article Text:
Yellow crazy ants (Anoplolepis gracilipes). Credits - Wikimedia Commons

How a tiny ant nearly wiped out a seabird colony

Bringing in dogs to catch what humans could not

The red-tailed tropic bird (Phaethon rubricauda) swarmed by yellow crazy ants (Anoplolepis gracilipes). Credits – Wikimedia Commons

What happens next for the recovering colony

After more than ten years of eradication work, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service declared Johnston Atoll free of yellow crazy ants, allowing red-tailed tropicbirds to nest again on land that had been unusable for years. The announcement, made in 2021, was the first time an invasive ant species had been fully eradicated from such a large area of land anywhere in the United States.Johnston Atoll sits roughly 1,320 kilometres southwest of Honolulu and forms part of the Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument, one of the most isolated stretches of land on the planet. According to the refuge's own page on the US Fish and Wildlife Service website , the atoll is home to one of the largest known nesting populations of red-tailed tropicbirds anywhere in the world, alongside more than 300 species of fish and a shallow coral reef spanning roughly 32,000 acres. That isolation, which normally protects the atoll's wildlife, became a liability when yellow crazy ants arrived sometime before 2010; they may have been carried in on cargo or equipment from elsewhere in the Pacific.Yellow crazy ants do not bite or sting in the way many people expect from ants, but their real weapon is even more disruptive. When threatened or present in large numbers, the ants spray formic acid on nearby animals, causing blindness, injuries and, in many cases, death among ground-nesting seabirds on Johnston Atoll.As the infestation spread across roughly 70 acres of the 640-acre refuge, it effectively wiped out red-tailed tropicbird nesting across that entire zone, since the birds could not raise chicks on ground regularly swarmed by ants spraying acid on anything that moved.The scale of the threat pushed the Fish and Wildlife Service to launch what became known as the Crazy Ant Strike Team, a rotating volunteer operation that ran continuously for a decade. The agency's own account of the project says nearly 100 staff and volunteers worked across 20 separate crews, each deployed for six-month stretches, and collectively logged more than 130,000 field hours battling the ants across the atoll. Crews experimented continuously with different bait formulations to find a treatment potent enough to eliminate the ants without causing wider harm to the atoll's other wildlife, then followed every round of bait treatment with repeated hand searches of the island to track down any ants that had survived.In the final stretch of the eradication campaign, crews used a surprising tactic borrowed from customs and search-and-rescue work rather than traditional pest control. In December 2020, the refuge brought in two conservation detection dogs specifically trained to sniff out yellow crazy ants, giving crews a far more sensitive tool than the human eye for confirming whether any pockets of the ants remained hidden in vegetation or debris after years of bait treatments. Using bait treatments, hand searches and canine detection over a decade, the Fish and Wildlife Service eventually confirmed the ants were gone.Kate Toniolo, superintendent for the Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument, said the eradication marked the first time an invasive ant species had been removed from such a large land area anywhere in the United States, crediting the result to the volunteers, staff and partners who carried out the decade-long effort.With the ants gone, attention on Johnston Atoll has shifted from eradication to recovery and long-term prevention. Officials have said the eradication ranks among the most significant invasive ant removals ever completed on a tropical island, given the scale of the 640-acre refuge involved. At the time, the Fish and Wildlife Service said its focus would shift to restoring habitat across the previously infested zone and preventing any future introduction of invasive species, since a single new arrival could undo more than a decade of painstaking work.For the seabirds, the change is already visible on the ground. Areas that were once too dangerous for chicks to survive are gradually reopening to nesting, and biologists monitoring the refuge expect the tropicbird colony, counted at nearly 13,000 nesting pairs in 2021, to keep expanding into that reclaimed territory in the seasons ahead. It is a gradual victory, measured in each patch of ground where chicks can now hatch safely.
Article Summary: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service declared Johnston Atoll free of yellow crazy ants in 2021. It was the first time an invasive ant species had been fully eradicated from such a large area of land anywhere in the United States. The atoll is home to one of the largest known nesting populations of red-tailed tropicbirds in the world.

Article Title: Pakistan: Security official killed by unidentified gunmen; 5 cops injured in separate grenade blast
Article Text:
According to police, two unidentified armed men targeted the security official. (Photo credit: IANS)

Five policemen injured in grenade attack

A security official was killed on Sunday after unidentified gunmen opened fire in northwest Pakistan, police said, according to news agency PTI.The incident took place within the jurisdiction of Badaber Police Station on the outskirts of Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.According to police, two unidentified armed men riding a motorcycle targeted the official, who was posted with the Counter Terrorism Department.He was killed on the spot, while the assailants fled the scene following the attack. Police cordoned off the area and launched a search operation to trace the attackers.No individual or group has so far claimed responsibility for the attack.In a separate incident in Mohmand district, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil, police said.Police retaliated with gunfire, forcing the attackers to flee. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger. An investigation is underway.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which borders Afghanistan, has witnessed recurring militant violence, cross-border movement of fighters and military operations.Pakistan's federal government has blamed the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) for attacks in areas bordering Afghanistan since a ceasefire agreement between the two sides ended in November 2022.
Article Summary: A security official was killed on Sunday after unidentified gunmen opened fire in northwest Pakistan. In a separate incident, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger.

Article Title: Destroyed in Operation Sindoor, JeM's Bahawalpur terror base fully operational again
Article Text:
Intelligence reports indicate that Pakistani authorities channeled 250 million PKR in cash to JeM,

Fresh footage indicates it is fully operational again, complete with reconstructed domes.

ALSO READ |

NEW DELHI: Extensive restoration work has concluded at the Markaz Subhanallah facility, the primary base for the UN-sanctioned terrorist group Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM), a little over a year after the compound suffered severe structural destruction during India's Operation Sindoor retaliatory strikes.Fresh footage indicates it is fully operational again, complete with reconstructed domes, updated interior plastering, new paint, and premium marble flooring that conceals previous blast damage.Deep blast zones within the primary hall were filled with concrete, while ruined satellite buildings—including the Al-Sabir seminary and housing units for leadership—were demolished to enable new construction.Intelligence reports indicate that Pakistani authorities channeled 250 million PKR in cash to JeM, with approximately 110 million PKR dedicated specifically to restoring the central complex over a 15-month period.With JeM leader Masood Azhar incapacitated by health issues, day-to-day command of the Bahawalpur facility has shifted to his brothers, Talha Al-Saif and Mohinuddin Aurangzeb (also known as Ammar Alvi).Meanwhile, senior figures Masood Azhar and Rauf Asghar remain harbored under government protection in the Nawabshah district of Sindh, sources said.
Article Summary: Extensive restoration work has concluded at the Markaz Subhanallah facility, the primary base for the UN-sanctioned terrorist group Jaish-e-Mohammed. The compound suffered severe structural destruction during India's Operation Sindoor retaliatory strikes.

Article Title: Pakistan power crisis: Karachi residents riot amid outages lasting hours, block major roads
Article Text:
Protesters blocked major roads and intersections, burned tyres and clashed with K-Electric personnel over prolonged blackouts (ANI photo)

Power protests erupted across several parts of Karachi as residents took to the streets over prolonged and unannounced outages, blocking major roads and burning tyres while demanding restoration of electricity.Demonstrations were reported in Pak Colony, Liaquatabad, Gharibabad, Nishtar Road, Bhimpura and Ranchore Line, disrupting traffic across key parts of Pakistan’s commercial capital. In Liaquatabad, protesters blocked major intersections, while clashes between traders and K-Electric (KE) staff over outages escalated into tyre-burning on Nishtar Road, as reported by local news outle Dawn.Residents said they were facing 12 hours or more of daily power cuts, often without adequate notice. The outages have also disrupted water supplies as pumping stations remain shut when electricity is unavailable, adding to public anger.“Bill-paying citizens are being punished with 12-hour load-shedding,” a protester in Liaquatabad said.The crisis also hit businesses and households, with residents reporting spoiled food, disrupted studies and sleepless nights as fans remained unusable during blackouts.The protests compounded an already severe traffic situation in the city. Roads were also closed for traditional Chup Tazia processions, while the power protests triggered additional blockades. Traffic police diverted vehicles to alternative routes, but those too became congested.Asif Khan, a private-sector employee, told Dawn he took four hours to travel from SITE to Liaquatabad after leaving work around 5pm. Another commuter said an ambulance carrying his feverish mother was stuck for about two hours near Civic Centre while they were travelling to a doctor in Saddar.“We pay bills on time but still face 12-hour power outages. Today we couldn’t even reach home,” commuter Imran from Gharibabad said.KE, however, attributed the prolonged outages in some affected areas to electricity theft and unpaid bills. A company spokesperson said outstanding dues from defaulters in Bandhani Colony and Rexer Line had crossed PKR 3 billion, adding that the duration of load-shedding depended on “electricity theft and the level of losses in the area”.The protests come as Karachi continues to grapple with an electricity crisis that is also affecting water supply, businesses and daily life across densely populated neighbourhoods.
Article Summary: Demonstrations reported in Pak Colony, Liaquatabad, Gharibabad, Nishtar Road, Bhimpura and Ranchore Line. Protesters blocked major roads and intersections, burned tyres and clashed with K-Electric personnel. Residents said they were facing 12 hours or more of daily power cuts, often without adequate notice.

Article Title: 'India could use water as weapon': Pakistan minister as Indus Waters Treaty remains in abeyance
Article Text:
Pakistan minister Ahsan Iqbal (File photo)

Pakistan minister Ahsan Iqbal has said India could “weaponise” the Indus Water Treaty (IWT) and expressed hope that “better sense” would prevail to prevent the two neighbours from going to war again, this time over water.He noted that the treaty had remained “untouchable” for almost seven decades since it was signed in 1960, but New Delhi has now been kept in abeyance “unilaterally."“...Indus Water Treaty that has stood the test of time for the last 70 years. India and Pakistan fought several wars, but it (IWT) was considered untouchable because it is an international agreement, and this time around the Indian government has unilaterally held it in abeyance... first time probably water has been weaponised in history,” Iqbal told the Asia Society.“We (Pakistan) now face this threat that they (India) can use water as a weapon to deny Pakistan when it needs it for its crops and release it when we don't need it... We are using all the diplomatic means to make sure that we don't have future wars on water because we have already seen lots of wars,” the minister added.He further stated that South Asian countries should instead focus on issues such as development, poverty, illiteracy and the youth “bulge”, describing the region as the “least integrated” in the world."So we hope that there is better sense in our neighbour's (India) mind and we don't see that water is weaponised and we go to another conflict with India over water because Pakistan cannot surrender at any cost the future of its 250 million people for its food security and right of water. If we let it happen, then every state that is on the lower side of water supply would be hostage to any country that controls the rivers," the Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz) leader remarked.Iqbal's remarks came days after Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif warned India of a “direct response” for putting the IWT in abeyance.“India proved itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. I declare in clear terms that every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. If India does not come to its senses, it will be responded to directly,” Sharif said on August 13, on the eve of Pakistan's Independence Day.New Delhi put the agreement in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year. Since then, Pakistani leaders have repeatedly called water their “red line” and threatened India over the move, describing it as an “act of war.”
Article Summary: Ahsan Iqbal says India could use water as a weapon to deny Pakistan when it needs it for its crops. New Delhi put the agreement in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year. Pakistani leaders have repeatedly called water their “red line” and threatened India.

Article Title: ‘In contempt for gathering people’: Pak blames ex PM Imran Khan’s party for hospital transfer
Article Text:
Pakistan government statement on Imran Khan's hospital transfer

Poll Vote & Share your view How do you view the involvement of PTI workers during Imran Khan transfer to the hospital? Justified, they were supporting their leader Unsure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Govt says court order was followed

NEW DELHI: The Pakistan government on Saturday blamed jailed former prime minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party for his transfer to a state-run hospital instead of the private facility ordered by the Supreme Court for his medical checkup.Information minister Attaullah Tarar said the government was forced to take 73-year-old Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) after a large number of PTI workers gathered outside Shifa International Hospital.The development came after Khan’s sister, Uzma Khan, approached the Supreme Court alleging that the government and senior officials had violated its order to shift the former prime minister to the private hospital.The Supreme Court had on August 18 directed authorities to transfer Khan from Adiala jail to Shifa Hospital within two days and keep him there until the next hearing on September 16. Instead, Khan was taken to PIMS and later returned to jail after doctors declared him fit.Tarar alleged that PTI workers gathered along the route to Shifa Hospital, removed barriers and created social media content, leaving authorities with no option but to shift Khan elsewhere.“Contempt has definitely happened,” Tarar said, accusing Khan’s sister and PTI of violating the court’s directions by turning the medical checkup into a political issue.The minister maintained that the government had implemented the Supreme Court’s order “in letter and spirit”. He said the medical examination was conducted transparently, Khan’s sister was present and doctors from Shifa Hospital were involved in the process.The Supreme Court’s order followed months of concerns raised by Khan’s family and supporters over his health, particularly an eye condition diagnosed earlier this year. Khan was taken to PIMS several times after being diagnosed with right central retinal vein occlusion in late January.A report submitted by jail authorities to the Supreme Court said his eye condition had improved significantly and that his vision was “almost normal”.Khan has been lodged in Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail since 2023 in connection with several cases.
Article Summary: Pakistan government blames jailed former prime minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party for his transfer to a state-run hospital. Information minister Attaullah Tarar said the government was forced to take 73-year-old Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences. Tarar alleged that PTI workers gathered along the route to Shifa Hospital, removed barriers and created social media content.

Article Title: Big crisis brewing in Rawalpindi? Pakistan deploys army for ‘sensitive duties’
Article Text:
The decision comes days after a man allegedly linked to former prime minister Imran Khan's party.

Army deployment follows security incident

Rawalpindi has strategic importance

The Pakistan government has authorised the deployment of the army in Rawalpindi for six months following a request from the Punjab home department for what it described as "sensitive security duties".The decision allows three companies of the Pakistan Army to be deployed in the city under Article 245 of the Pakistani Constitution, which permits the armed forces to assist the civil administration in maintaining security."The federal government, exercising the powers conferred under Article 245 of the Constitution of Pakistan, is pleased to authorise the deployment of three companies of the Pakistan Army for sensitive security duties in Rawalpindi," according to a notification issued by the Ministry of Interior and Narcotics Control on Friday.The notification said the deployment was intended to prevent a potential security problem and ensure that authorities could respond quickly if an unexpected situation arose.It said that the decision was taken "to avoid any undesirable situation as well as to respond effectively in any unforeseen situation as per the requirement of the district administration".The decision comes days after a man allegedly linked to former prime minister Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party opened fire at security forces in Rawalpindi.He was subsequently killed in retaliatory firing.State-run PTV News, citing security sources, reported that the attacker was a resident of Khyber district and an "active PTI member". According to the report, a PTI flag, bullets and weapons were recovered from him.The PTI, however, rejected any connection with the incident. The party said it had nothing to do with terrorism and accused authorities of attempting to associate the party with the attack.The deployment is particularly significant because Rawalpindi is home to the Pakistan Army's General Headquarters, the military's top command centre.The city is therefore an important military and administrative centre, and the decision to deploy army personnel there comes amid heightened security concerns following the recent shooting incident.The deployment has been authorised for six months, with the troops to perform duties requested by the district administration under the constitutional provision allowing the military to assist civilian authorities.
Article Summary: Three companies of the Pakistan Army will be deployed in Rawalpindi for six months. The decision comes after a man allegedly linked to Imran Khan's party opened fire in the city. The deployment is intended to prevent a potential security problem and ensure that authorities can respond quickly.

Article Title: 'Repeatedly tortured': Imran Khan's sister alleges abuse in jail as ex-Pakistan PM returns to prison
Article Text:
‘He was repeatedly tortured in jail’: Imran Khan's sister alleges mistreatment

PTI files contempt petition

Supporters gather after brief hospital visit

Pakistan's jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan repeatedly told his sister that he was being tortured in prison, she said on Saturday, a day after he was taken to a state-run hospital for a brief medical examination and sent back to jail.Khan's sister, Uzma Khan, attended his examination at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad and said the former prime minister was physically fit but had repeatedly complained of torture.“Khan told me that he is being repeatedly tortured in prison”, she told the media.The interior and law ministries, along with jail authorities, have not responded to a Reuters request for comment on the allegation.Khan was taken to PIMS overnight on Friday after the Supreme Court had directed authorities to transfer him from Adiala jail to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for a medical examination. He was declared medically fit and returned to prison within hours.Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party on Saturday filed a contempt petition against the government, accusing authorities of violating the Supreme Court's order by taking him to PIMS instead of the private hospital named by the court.The petition seeks action against senior government officials and asks that Khan be taken to Shifa International Hospital for treatment, PTI legal adviser Naeem Panjutha said."The petition seeks action against the ​prime minister, law minister, information minister" and other government officials, Panjutha said, adding that it also calls for Khan's treatment at the private hospital ordered by the court.The PTI also alleged that Khan was denied access to his personal physician, which it said amounted to another breach of the Supreme Court's directive.A three-judge Supreme Court bench had on Tuesday directed authorities to transfer Khan from Adiala jail to Shifa International Hospital within two days for a medical examination.The PTI interprets the order as requiring Khan to remain under medical supervision until at least mid-September.Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the decision to take Khan to PIMS instead of the court-named private hospital was made because of security concerns.Khan declared medically fit, sent back to jailKhan was examined by a team of doctors, including an ophthalmologist, cardiologist and physician, before being declared medically fit and sent back to Adiala jail in Rawalpindi."A team of qualified doctors, including an ophthalmologist, a cardiologist and a physician conducted a detailed examination of him and declared him medically fit," Tarar said.Khan has been imprisoned since August 2023 and maintains that the cases against him are politically motivated. The government denies the allegation.His lawyers have previously said his health has deteriorated in prison and that he has suffered substantial loss of vision in his right eye. The government has maintained that medical reports have found no condition requiring immediate treatment.Khan's supporters gathered along roads in Islamabad overnight, throwing flowers at a vehicle believed to be carrying him to the hospital.The scenes were broadcast live on Pakistani television, in a notable departure from recent years when broadcasters often avoided mentioning Khan's name.PTI leaders have warned that the latest developments could increase pressure on the government and fuel fresh demonstrations."After what happened yesterday, the pressure (on authorities) will double," Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi said, adding that preparations for a protest march planned for September 27 had picked up.Khan's arrest and imprisonment have remained a major source of political tension in Pakistan. His arrest in 2023 triggered widespread protests, including attacks on military installations, and his supporters continue to demand his release.
Article Summary: Imran Khan repeatedly told his sister that he was being tortured in prison, she says. Khan was taken to a state-run hospital for a brief medical examination and sent back to jail. He was declared medically fit and returned to prison within hours. Khan has been imprisoned since August 2023 and maintains that the cases against him are politically motivated.

Article Title: Imran Khan's kin say Pak govt violated court order for not taking ex-PM to private hospital
Article Text:
Imran Khan shifted back to jail after medical examination

Family alleges violation of court order

NEW DELHI: Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan was shifted back to Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi early Friday, hours after he was taken for a medical examination amid a legal battle over his health and demands from his family and supporters for better medical care.Khan, 73, was taken to the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad, Pakistan's information minister Attaullah Tarar said, news agaency PTI reports. The government later said Khan was medically fit and returned him to jail at around 5 am.The development came days after the Supreme Court ordered authorities to move Khan to Al-Shifa hospital following a medical report that said he was suffering from “level three plus” anxiety.Khan's family has repeatedly raised concerns about his access to adequate medical treatment while in custody. His sister, Uzma Khan, was present during the medical examination at PIMS, according to AP. They have accused authorities of violating a court order by taking him to a government hospital for a medical examination instead of a private hospital designated by the court.She alleged that during their meeting, Khan complained of being kept in solitary confinement, which she described as “mental torture” for the former prime minister.Khan’s personal physician, Faisal Sultan, said he had been taken to Shifa International Hospital, where he waited for Khan until early Friday. He was later informed that Khan had instead been returned to Adiala prison in Rawalpindi.Tarar said authorities changed the plan because of security concerns after supporters of Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) gathered outside Shifa International Hospital or were heading there.Khan has been in custody since his arrest on August 5, 2023, in a corruption case.
Article Summary: Imran Khan, 73, was taken to the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad. The government later said Khan was medically fit and returned him to jail at around 5 am. The development came days after the Supreme Court ordered authorities to move Khan to Al-Shifa hospital.

Article Title: Ex-Pak PM Imran Khan moved to private hospital from prison after SC order
Article Text:
Imran Khan’s transfer follows months of health concerns, including a dispute over worsening vision in his right eye

Imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan was shifted from Adiala prison to a private hospital in Islamabad after midnight Thursday for a medical examination, news agency AP reported citing Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party's statement.Khan was taken to Shifa International Hospital hours after Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said the government would comply with a Supreme Court order directing authorities to facilitate his medical examination.The PTI said the transfer was carried out following the Supreme Court's order earlier this week but did not provide further details. It remained unclear whether Khan would return to prison after the examination or stay at the hospital for further treatment. His family and party have sought permission for him to remain there.Earlier Thursday, Chaudhry said the government had approached the Supreme Court seeking clarification on whether the medical relief granted to Khan applied only to him or could also cover other prisoners. He stressed that the request was not aimed at delaying or defying the court's order.The three-judge Supreme Court panel had ordered authorities two days earlier to take Khan to Shifa International Hospital for a medical examination amid prolonged concerns raised by his family and personal doctors over his health and access to treatment.The court directed that a medical board examine him, including specialists and his personal physician, Faisal Sultan.The government has maintained that prisoners receive medical care under existing rules and can be moved to government hospitals when required.Concerns over Khan's health intensified in January after his family claimed he had lost about 85% of the vision in his right eye. The government disputed the claim and later said his vision had improved by around 70%.Khan, a former cricket star, was ousted as prime minister in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. He has remained imprisoned since 2023 after convictions in multiple cases, including a graft case.
Article Summary: Imran Khan was moved from Adiala prison to a private hospital in Islamabad after midnight Thursday for a medical examination. It remained unclear whether Khan would return to prison after the examination or stay at the hospital for further treatment. His family and party have sought permission for him to remain there. Article Title: Red-faced Pakistan summons top diplomat over US envoy Gor's J&K remark in Srinagar
Article Text:
US Ambassador Sergio Gor visits Srinagar with J&K CM Omar

Pakistan on Wednesday summoned the top US diplomat Islamabad and lodged a protest after US envoy to India Sergio Gor described Jammu and Kashmir as an “important part of India” during his visit to Srinagar on Wednesday.The remarks came as Gor made his first visit to Jammu and Kashmir since taking office and met chief minister Omar Abdullah.Gor’s comments were made during a joint media briefing with Abdullah following their meeting at the chief minister’s residence. “It’s a pleasure to be here. This is an important part of India. I am here, visiting for the first time. It is an incredibly beautiful place. I am thrilled to be here,” the US envoy said.Gor also indicated that Washington could reconsider its travel advisory for Jammu and Kashmir, saying the US regularly reviews its warnings. He said the Indian government and the Jammu and Kashmir administration had taken steps to improve safety in the region.“I cannot make any big announcements here today, but it is something we are going to look at,” Gor said, adding that the US would consider whether its existing travel warning should be downgraded.The ambassador also described his meeting with Abdullah as “very good” and said the two sides had discussed ways to deepen economic cooperation and create opportunities benefiting India and the US.Abdullah said the talks focused on what Washington could do for Jammu and Kashmir, while also referring to “certain legacy issues” that would need to be addressed.“We look forward to taking this conversation further,” Abdullah said, adding that he was “very hopeful and optimistic” that engagement between the US and Jammu and Kashmir would “both widen and deepen in the years ahead”.
Article Summary: Pakistan summons top US diplomat Islamabad and lodges a protest. US envoy to India Sergio Gor described Jammu and Kashmir as an “important part of India’ Gor also indicated that Washington could reconsider its travel advisory for J&K.

Article Title: Pakistan govt to challenge SC order to move jailed ex-PM Imran Khan to hospital
Article Text:
'Not within four walls of law': Pak law minister on Khan hospitalisation order

The Shehbaz Sharif-led Pakistan government will challenge the Supreme Court's order directing the transfer of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan to a private hospital, as law minister Azam Nazeer Tarar confirmed in a video message on Wednesday.According to news agency Reuters, the Pakitan Supreme Court had ordered the government to move Khan to Islamabad’s Shifa International Hospital within two days and allow him access to his personal physician.“This order is not within four walls of the law,” Tarar said in a video statement.He said authorities had reviewed the ruling and decided to approach the court seeking a review. “A convicted prisoner has to be treated either inside the jail or at a public hospital according to law,” Tarar said, adding that the review petition would seek a modification of the order.The move could end hopes of Imran Khan’s family and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), which have repeatedly sought better healthcare and visitation rights for the former PM.It could also trigger public discontent over his treatment in custody.Recently, Imran Khan supporters staged widespread protest over his imprisonment against Islamabad government.Khan, 73, has been jailed in Rawalpindi since August 2023 after being convicted in several cases that he says are politically motivated.He was removed from office in 2022 after falling out with Pakistan's powerful military establishment under army chief Asim Munir's influence.The Supreme Court order came after former president Arif Alvi raised concerns over World Cup winning captain and former PM's medical condition.Alvi also shared Khan's vitals on X.Imran Khan's sons have also repeatedly expressed concern about his deteriorating health, while his lawyers have claimed he suffered significant vision loss in his right eye while in prison.
Article Summary: Pakistani law minister Azam Nazeer Tarar confirms government will challenge the Supreme Court's order. Khan, 73, has been jailed in Rawalpindi since August 2023 after being convicted in several cases. He was removed from office in 2022 after falling out with Pakistan's powerful military establishment.
